output.text_basic:
This question comes up often; often in discussions about the possibility of a complete disaster and how best to respond. The answer is going to vary a great deal depending on who is asking—the answer can be anything; from death to a change in routine. Obviously, the answer for my family is neither of those things.

The question is not only focused on the immediate impact of no electric, but also on how people will survive long term, if they survive at all. And you don’t need to be on a Prepper’s forum to stumble on such discussion.

Surprisingly, few people actually know where to start; and even fewer have a plan. Even fewer still have realistic plans that would allow them to survive beyond a few days. And those that do, often have unrealistic expectations that are going to fail them when push comes to shove.

This article aims to discuss and plan this scenario, and to help both readers that are looking into preparedness, as well as current preppers who might need to do a little adjustment on their plan.

Before I start with the explanation on how to survive after the electric grid is gone, I want to clarify the difference between blackouts due to failures during the day (most commonly), and blackouts that are due to total disaster (power grid failures in the wider sense).

I’m going to focus on the latter, for the sake of honest discussion, but much of what I’m going to discuss will still apply to the former—the difference is in the duration of blackouts and the amount of preparation required.

## How Would a Total Grid Collapse Impact My Life and Survival?

First, it’s important to understand that the impact is going to be much more than just the power going off. Think about how many things in your life rely on electricity; more importantly, consider things that rely on your ability to be plugged into the grid.

If you don’t have a backup plan that includes a generator and/or solar panels; or if you choose to ignore this article because “it won’t happen” and wait for services to be restored, you are making a grave mistake.

Consider everything that keeps running even when you are not home: A central heating/air conditioning system, water pump, refrigerator that keeps food fresh, septic tank, computer and internet, phone landline, cell phone charging, even home security systems and so on.

In a total grid collapse scenario, the first things to go after 24-48 hours are going to be the water and sewage services; because those are the easiest and the fastest to fail. This will bring about an immediate rise in waterborne diseases, and will quickly bring water scarcity in certain areas.

Next thing to go is going to be the food supply. Within the first week of no electricity, most food will be spoiled, and within 2 weeks, a lot of groceries will be out of stock and no one will be producing new ones for obvious reasons—with the lack of fuel and diesel in particular. As we saw during Hurricane Katrina, there are places where the damage wasn’t widespread and where services were restored relatively quickly, but the damage to the infrastructure has still caused long-lasting food shortages due to the logistical issues.

The consequences of a total grid collapse are catastrophic, especially in the first few months; but the aftermath is going to be just as deadly in some places.

The only people that will be safe are the ones that don’t rely on the grid for food and electricity, or the ones that were smart enough to prepare even if that means living in a remote location with no infrastructure whatsoever.

## Preparing for a Grid Collapse, Step by Step

It’s important to note that this article will focus on things that people can do in urban settings, both to survive and to prepare for an impending disaster. A lot of information out there will teach you how to live in the wilderness and hunt for your food, among other things.

These are valuable skills to learn, but they have limited real-world applications for urban survival because most of us live in cities or settlements and we have no desire to change that. If my survival requires me to leave the comforts of a city, the grid will be the least of my concern.

### 1. Finding Safety and Security

The first things we need to talk about are safety and security. After all, you can go without food for days and without water for weeks if needed; but you really can’t live without safety, and you can’t survive in hostile territory.

Safety in the wilderness means understanding the natural threats around you; which means being aware of wildlife and vegetation. In urban settings, the threats are more likely to be human in nature—theft, riots, and looting should be your first points of concern.

First, make sure to stay inside a sturdy, well-built home or a building—a basement, if possible. If you can, choose a safe neighborhood with little crime and heavy police presence.

Choose a neighborhood with plenty of natural barriers, such as dense vegetations, hills, parks or other areas that aren’t easily observed or easily accessed due to limited access routes. Avoid densely populated areas or areas with any sort of natural disaster risks—you don’t want to choose a place that is a potential flood risk or risk of falling buildings.

If riots and looting become an issue, it’s best to relocate, if possible. As much as you love your home, you need to stay safe and secure in such a situation. After a few days, things will calm down, and you can return to normal life.

In essence, your first priority should be to find the safest possible location in the city where you can safely stay until the riots calm down.

Once the police return, they are usually able to help. However, I want to warn you not to rely on them, especially in the immediate aftermath of a disaster. Some areas, even those that are considered safe, may also be controlled by other groups, and you don’t want to be caught in a crossfire. This is why having self-defense skills is important.

### 2. Building a Self-Sustaining Power and Water Supply

Next, you’re going to need to find or build a source of food, water, and heat. All of these are going to become scarce in the first part of the disaster, but eventually, you will find them. The key is to be able to store what you have and use it wisely.

First, let’s look into power and heat.

#### Power

The first thing that will come to mind when thinking about power supply are solar panels and generators—but those are only a short-term solution and only if backup fuel is available (generators don’t work without fuel or diesel).

The long-term solution to the power issue is having a generator capable of running on biofuel, charcoal, wood pellets, or animal fat. If you intend to stay for an extended period, you may also want to consider creating a steam engine with a generator attached to it.

Steam engines can use any sort of biomass, even garbage or sewage, but they need a great deal of space and plenty of equipment to operate; even then, they are only efficient with a continuous power output of a few hundred watts.

As you can see, generating power—especially in urban settings—is going to be a challenge. The biggest difficulty, however, is to store it efficiently.

Batteries are your best bet for storing power, and they need to be in large quantities because you’ll rely on them to power your lights, phone, radio, and other necessary electronics. A 200-watt steam engine can generate enough power to power 1 or 2 LED bulbs. Storing power in batteries is inefficient because they lose their storage capacity every time they are recharged.

Having a large number of batteries is more useful than using the same number of expensive, specialized batteries with limited lifespan.

I’ve found that the rechargeable AA batteries last the longest, but you’ll need around 80 AA batteries, with a 4000mAh battery and an average of 5 battery uses per day to maintain your electronics for even a short while.

On the other hand, the cheapest solution I’ve found is aluminum-metal-ion capacitors—a few of them can provide enough power to get you through an evening, and they can be reliably charged with the least amount of infrastructure.

#### Fuel

Fuel is going to be difficult to find because it has a multitude of uses, including powering the transportation fleet, lighting the homes—and, you’ve probably noticed, generating electricity.

If possible, find a place with plenty of wood, and build a wood-fired stove for heating, cooking, and boiling water. This will allow you to have access to clean, and hot water at all times. The stoves can also fuel the steam engine, and if necessary, they can burn just about any vegetation you have on hand, making them the perfect survival fire when it comes time to evacuate.

I recommend gathering wood early in the crisis; because woodlands are going to become the battleground as people start to starve, and it will become more and more difficult to maintain supplies.

The good news is that charcoal briquettes can last for months, if stored in a cool, dry place. However, you may not have the resources to burn them without a wood stove, grill, or barbecue. You can start fires with charcoal in dry weather, but it’s not practical, nor efficient.

If you don’t have the resources to store wood for boiling water by itself, you can burn dried leaves and tree bark because they are both common in the wilderness and have limited uses when it comes to cooking.

#### Water and Cooking

Water will become scarce as the grid collapses; people will start to worry, and water-related disorders will spread fast. To make sure you can safely drink water, you need to filter it; but I urge you not to rely on bottled water, even if you stockpile it now.

Bottled water will become a luxury after an emergency, and you will have trouble carrying the amounts needed even in the immediate aftermath.

Having a large tank for water storage, and a filtration system or UV filter is essential; it helps to remove the parasites and bacteria that can make you sick, allowing you to drink unpolluted groundwater or rainwater, as well as to reuse shower or bath water.

Furthermore, having a good cooking area can save the day as it will allow you to prepare hot food. If you don’t have the luxury of a wood stove, a single burner portable stove can easily be powered by charcoal briquettes.

The more self-sustaining solutions you build, the more secure you will be. Having everything set up, even if that is only a single burner, a battery of capacitors, a few large bottles of drinking water, and some supplies, is better than nothing.

#### Food

Preparing enough food for an extended period of time is quite the challenge in urban settings. Food requires a great deal of energy and water for its acquisition, storage, and preparation.

The only real solution I’ve found for urban survival is to have a well-stocked food pantry, with a few months’ worth of supplies. After that, you need to rely on hunting and foraging to find food on a daily basis.

It’s difficult to explain, but having a few months’ worth of supplies is essential to your survival. As supplies dwindle and the riots begin, it will be difficult to venture out and forage for food; but it will be downright dangerous to try and go hunting.

In an urban setting, you have a wide variety of opportunities in terms of food sources, but they are all going to be gone, and unless you know how to forage for food, you will be in serious trouble.

Learning to forage for food will save your life if times get rough; because even a single meal can be a life-saver when the food supplies are gone. The good news is that there are plenty of resources on foraging for food on the internet. I’ll include several at the end of the article if you want to learn more about this important skill for urban preppers.

Finally, I have to mention the importance of a well-equipped hunting kit, with a good hunting rifle, 10 or 12 boxes of ammo, and at least a dozen steel traps. With these few items, and some practice, you can feed your family for at least a month.

### 3. Understand Social Behavior in Emergency Situations

If the grid goes out, there may be little law enforcement or organized response to the crisis. People’s reactions are going to dictate the severity of the immediate aftermath, and they will also impact how you and your family survive.

The best way I’ve learned to deal with social situations is to look towards nature and see how other mammals act when they are faced with death. The fight or flight response is the way the mammalian brain reacts to stress; and the body’s response is usually either to engage the threat (fight) or run away from it (flight).

Both of these responses are driven by survival instincts and are usually the right choice. However, they can also lead to the downfall of an entire community if they are not controlled.

In emergency situations, people are usually divided into 4 categories:

1. Those that take care of their families and neighbors;
2. Those that take advantage of the situation and take what they can;

8. Tools: A basic tool kit can be invaluable in a blackout. This could include a multi-tool, pocket knife, flashlight, batteries, and other items that could assist with survival tasks.

Question: If all electricity was cut off, how would you survive?
Answer: 

This question comes up often; often in discussions about the possibility of a complete disaster and how best to respond. The answer is going to vary a great deal depending on who is asking—the answer can be anything; from death to a change in routine. Obviously, the answer for my family is neither of those things.

The question is not only focused on the immediate impact of no electric, but also on how people will survive long term, if they survive at all. And you don’t need to be on a Prepper’s forum to stumble on such discussion.

Surprisingly, few people actually know where to start; and even fewer have a plan. Even fewer still have realistic plans that would allow them to survive beyond a few days. And those that do, often have unrealistic expectations that are going to fail them when push comes to shove.

This article aims to discuss and plan this scenario, and to help both readers that are looking into preparedness, as well as current preppers who might need to do a little adjustment on their plan.

Before I start with the explanation on how to survive after the electric grid is gone, I want to clarify the difference between blackouts due to failures during the day (most commonly), and blackouts that are due to total disaster (power grid failures in the wider sense).

I’m going to focus on the latter, for the sake of honest discussion, but much of what I’m going to discuss will still apply to the former—the difference is in the duration of blackouts and the amount of preparation required.

## How Would a Total Grid Collapse Impact My Life and Survival?

First, it’s important to understand that the impact is going to be much more than just the power going off. Think about how many things in your life rely on electricity; more importantly, consider things that rely on your ability to be plugged into the grid.

If you don’t have a backup plan that includes a generator and/or solar panels; or if you choose to ignore this article because “it won’t happen” and wait for services to be restored, you are making a grave mistake.

Consider everything that keeps running even when you are not home: A central heating/air conditioning system, water pump, refrigerator that keeps food fresh, septic tank, computer and internet, phone landline, cell phone charging, even home security systems and so on.

In a total grid collapse scenario, the first things to go after 24-48 hours are going to be the water and sewage services; because those are the easiest and the fastest to fail. This will bring about an immediate rise in waterborne diseases, and will quickly bring water scarcity in certain areas.

Next thing to go is going to be the food supply. Within the first week of no electricity, most food will be spoiled, and within 2 weeks, a lot of groceries will be out of stock and no one will be producing new ones for obvious reasons—with the lack of fuel and diesel in particular. As we saw during Hurricane Katrina, there are places where the damage wasn’t widespread and where services were restored relatively quickly, but the damage to the infrastructure has still caused long-lasting food shortages due to the logistical issues.

The consequences of a total grid collapse are catastrophic, especially in the first few months; but the aftermath is going to be just as deadly in some places.

The only people that will be safe are the ones that don’t rely on the grid for food and electricity, or the ones that were smart enough to prepare even if that means living in a remote location with no infrastructure whatsoever.

## Preparing for a Grid Collapse, Step by Step

It’s important to note that this article will focus on things that people can do in urban settings, both to survive and to prepare for an impending disaster. A lot of information out there will teach you how to live in the wilderness and hunt for your food, among other things.

These are valuable skills to learn, but they have limited real-world applications for urban survival because most of us live in cities or settlements and we have no desire to change that. If my survival requires me to leave the comforts of a city, the grid will be the least of my concern.

### 1. Finding Safety and Security

The first things we need to talk about are safety and security. After all, you can go without food for days and without water for weeks if needed; but you really can’t live without safety, and you can’t survive in hostile territory.

Safety in the wilderness means understanding the natural threats around you; which means being aware of wildlife and vegetation. In urban settings, the threats are more likely to be human in nature—theft, riots, and looting should be your first points of concern.

First, make sure to stay inside a sturdy, well-built home or a building—a basement, if possible. If you can, choose a safe neighborhood with little crime and heavy police presence.

Choose a neighborhood with plenty of natural barriers, such as dense vegetations, hills, parks or other areas that aren’t easily observed or easily accessed due to limited access routes. Avoid densely populated areas or areas with any sort of natural disaster risks—you don’t want to choose a place that is a potential flood risk or risk of falling buildings.

If riots and looting become an issue, it’s best to relocate, if possible. As much as you love your home, you need to stay safe and secure in such a situation. After a few days, things will calm down, and you can return to normal life.

In essence, your first priority should be to find the safest possible location in the city where you can safely stay until the riots calm down.

Once the police return, they are usually able to help. However, I want to warn you not to rely on them, especially in the immediate aftermath of a disaster. Some areas, even those that are considered safe, may also be controlled by other groups, and you don’t want to be caught in a crossfire. This is why having self-defense skills is important.

### 2. Building a Self-Sustaining Power and Water Supply

Next, you’re going to need to find or build a source of food, water, and heat. All of these are going to become scarce in the first part of the disaster, but eventually, you will find them. The key is to be able to store what you have and use it wisely.

First, let’s look into power and heat.

#### Power

The first thing that will come to mind when thinking about power supply are solar panels and generators—but those are only a short-term solution and only if backup fuel is available (generators don’t work without fuel or diesel).

The long-term solution to the power issue is having a generator capable of running on biofuel, charcoal, wood pellets, or animal fat. If you intend to stay for an extended period, you may also want to consider creating a steam engine with a generator attached to it.

Steam engines can use any sort of biomass, even garbage or sewage, but they need a great deal of space and plenty of equipment to operate; even then, they are only efficient with a continuous power output of a few hundred watts.

As you can see, generating power—especially in urban settings—is going to be a challenge. The biggest difficulty, however, is to store it efficiently.

Batteries are your best bet for storing power, and they need to be in large quantities because you’ll rely on them to power your lights, phone, radio, and other necessary electronics. A 200-watt steam engine can generate enough power to power 1 or 2 LED bulbs. Storing power in batteries is inefficient because they lose their storage capacity every time they are recharged.

Having a large number of batteries is more useful than using the same number of expensive, specialized batteries with limited lifespan.

I’ve found that the rechargeable AA batteries last the longest, but you’ll need around 80 AA batteries, with a 4000mAh battery and an average of 5 battery uses per day to maintain your electronics for even a short while.

On the other hand, the cheapest solution I’ve found is aluminum-metal-ion capacitors—a few of them can provide enough power to get you through an evening, and they can be reliably charged with the least amount of infrastructure.

#### Fuel

Fuel is going to be difficult to find because it has a multitude of uses, including powering the transportation fleet, lighting the homes—and, you’ve probably noticed, generating electricity.

If possible, find a place with plenty of wood, and build a wood-fired stove for heating, cooking, and boiling water. This will allow you to have access to clean, and hot water at all times. The stoves can also fuel the steam engine, and if necessary, they can burn just about any vegetation you have on hand, making them the perfect survival fire when it comes time to evacuate.

I recommend gathering wood early in the crisis; because woodlands are going to become the battleground as people start to starve, and it will become more and more difficult to maintain supplies.

The good news is that charcoal briquettes can last for months, if stored in a cool, dry place. However, you may not have the resources to burn them without a wood stove, grill, or barbecue. You can start fires with charcoal in dry weather, but it’s not practical, nor efficient.

If you don’t have the resources to store wood for boiling water by itself, you can burn dried leaves and tree bark because they are both common in the wilderness and have limited uses when it comes to cooking.

#### Water and Cooking

Water will become scarce as the grid collapses; people will start to worry, and water-related disorders will spread fast. To make sure you can safely drink water, you need to filter it; but I urge you not to rely on bottled water, even if you stockpile it now.

Bottled water will become a luxury after an emergency, and you will have trouble carrying the amounts needed even in the immediate aftermath.

Having a large tank for water storage, and a filtration system or UV filter is essential; it helps to remove the parasites and bacteria that can make you sick, allowing you to drink unpolluted groundwater or rainwater, as well as to reuse shower or bath water.

Furthermore, having a good cooking area can save the day as it will allow you to prepare hot food. If you don’t have the luxury of a wood stove, a single burner portable stove can easily be powered by charcoal briquettes.

The more self-sustaining solutions you build, the more secure you will be. Having everything set up, even if that is only a single burner, a battery of capacitors, a few large bottles of drinking water, and some supplies, is better than nothing.

#### Food

Preparing enough food for an extended period of time is quite the challenge in urban settings. Food requires a great deal of energy and water for its acquisition, storage, and preparation.

The only real solution I’ve found for urban survival is to have a well-stocked food pantry, with a few months’ worth of supplies. After that, you need to rely on hunting and foraging to find food on a daily basis.

It’s difficult to explain, but having a few months’ worth of supplies is essential to your survival. As supplies dwindle and the riots begin, it will be difficult to venture out and forage for food; but it will be downright dangerous to try and go hunting.

In an urban setting, you have a wide variety of opportunities in terms of food sources, but they are all going to be gone, and unless you know how to forage for food, you will be in serious trouble.

Learning to forage for food will save your life if times get rough; because even a single meal can be a life-saver when the food supplies are gone. The good news is that there are plenty of resources on foraging for food on the internet. I’ll include several at the end of the article if you want to learn more about this important skill for urban preppers.

Finally, I have to mention the importance of a well-equipped hunting kit, with a good hunting rifle, 10 or 12 boxes of ammo, and at least a dozen steel traps. With these few items, and some practice, you can feed your family for at least a month.

### 3. Understand Social Behavior in Emergency Situations

If the grid goes out, there may be little law enforcement or organized response to the crisis. People’s reactions are going to dictate the severity of the immediate aftermath, and they will also impact how you and your family survive.

5. Communication: In a blackout, traditional phone lines may also be affected. If you have a charged mobile phone, you might still be able to send text messages or use data to communicate.

6. Warmth: Heat is crucial, especially in colder climates. Fireplaces or wood-burning stoves can be useful, but ensure you have a good supply of wood. Warm clothing and extra blankets can also help.

7. First Aid: A well-stocked first aid kit is essential in any emergency. In a blackout, it could be used to treat injuries or conditions that might arise.

8. Tools: A basic tool kit can be invaluable in a blackout. This could include a multi-tool, pocket knife, flashlight, batteries, and other items that could assist with survival tasks.

Surviving a complete blackout for an extended period would be extremely challenging, and it's crucial to remember that the situation could affect the entire community. If possible, try to work together with neighbors to share resources and support each other.

To treat a common cold, the goal is to boost the body's immune system, reduce symptoms such as congestion, and manage discomfort.

1. Rest: Rest is crucial to aid the immune system in fighting off the cold. Encourage plenty of sleep and reduce physical activities.

2. Hydrate: Drink lots of fluids to stay hydrated. Water, tea with honey, and warm lemon water can help soothe sore throats and ease congestion.

3. Humidify: Use a humidifier to add moisture to the air, which can help thin mucus and make breathing easier.

4. Steam: Inhale steam from a bowl of hot water or a hot shower to help ease nasal congestion and soothe a sore throat.

5. Vitamin C: Although it might not shorten the duration of a cold, it may help reduce the severity of symptoms. Foods high in vitamin C include citrus fruits, strawberries, bell peppers, and broccoli.

6. Zinc: Zinc can help reduce the length of a cold if taken within 24 hours of first experiencing symptoms. You can find zinc in foods such as beef, oysters, and peanuts. Some supplements are also available.

7. Ginger: Ginger can help fight inflammation and has been shown to relieve some cold symptoms. Ginger tea with honey or adding grated ginger to hot water and lemon can be beneficial.

8. Echinacea: While research on echinacea for treating colds is inconclusive, some people find it helpful in reducing symptoms and boosting the immune system when taken as a supplement.

9. Elderberry: Elderberry syrup or extract is believed to boost the immune system and shorten the duration of colds.

10. Over-the-counter remedies: Although I've been focusing on alternative methods, over-the-counter medicines such as decongestants, pain relievers, and cough suppressants may provide temporary relief of symptoms. 8. Echinacea: While research on echinacea for treating colds is inconclusive, some people find it helpful in reducing symptoms and boosting the immune system when taken as a supplement.

input.text_cot: If there were no more planes, how would you travel to another continent? Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
Cale looked at the other travelers, who were all staring at the same map, hanging on the wall of the airport with a sense of fear. The map was huge, it covered the entire north wall and was so detailed that you could pinpoint exactly where you were in the world.

"What continent do we want to go to?" Cale said with a frown.

"Asia, I think." Han, the Asian-looking traveler, stepped forward to answer.

"Oh, that's easy. Just follow the map."

"It's not just as easy as that anymore." Han looked back at Cale and shook his head. "Aren't you reading the news? A large part of the world's air transport network is shut down right now, planes are being stolen all over the world."

"The world? But what is going on exactly?"

"Do you remember the news report on the BBC World News about 'Hijackers in Planes'?"

"Oh, the one where they said a group of terrorists were controlling the passengers using a remote control that could hack and control aircraft computer systems?"

"Yes, the one that has created fear all over the world, turning every plane into a potential target."

Cale took a step back and looked around. This was not what he expected. He had arrived in Istanbul just over a week ago, only to find that the world had changed overnight. Now he was stuck with several other travelers with the goal of reaching Asia. What awaited them on the other side of the world was still a mystery, but there was no choice left but to set out regardless.

Han was speaking again, "We saw a group of travelers who said they made it to the mountains of Nepal and it is said that a group of people in Nepal are planning to set off on an expedition to Tibet."

"Tibet..." Cale repeated weakly, looking at the mountains on the huge map.

The mountains were close, the road passed through Turkey, then passed over the Caspian Sea, into Kazakhstan and then crossed the Hindu Kush range. In front of Cale and his companions, it seemed like a long and dangerous journey.

"Let's look for a way." Cale moved closer to the map, looking at the various roads and transportation routes available to them. "Let's start with the easiest transport option in the region, but it's a long journey."

"What do you have in mind?"

"We can start walking along the Trans-Anatolian railway or we can go overland and follow the Silk Road, it's almost the same path."

"But the Silk Road was used by the Chinese thousands of years ago, do they still use it?"

"It's still being used, even if only by a few, and there is even an ancient Chinese route that goes directly from Istanbul to Tibet."

"But this journey will take months, surely there's a different route?"

"If we use airplanes, of course there are other routes, but now that's not an option."

"We have no choice, let's leave for Ankara, we can find something in Ankara."

With that decision made, they set off with their backpacks towards the capital city of Turkey, Ankara, the first stop on their journey.

* * *

Walking along the streets of Ankara, Cale felt a strange sensation, as if the earth were breathing, the rhythm of the street seemed to pulse. As he walked with his traveler companions, he found it increasingly difficult to believe that it was this very city that was causing the world's air transport network to shrink.

"What are those buildings?" Cale asked, pointing at a group of large buildings.

"Those are the Turkish Airlines Headquarters, this one looks like a spaceship." Ahmet, one of Cale's companions, explained.

"Is it true that they have been closed for months? Why can't they fly now?"

"Yes, they have been closed for months. It all started when some terrorists took over three Turkish Airlines planes at the beginning of October. Two were hijacked at the Istanbul airport while the third was hijacked over the Black Sea."

"That was in October, but we just found out a few days ago that planes are being hijacked all over the world, how did that happen?"

"This has been going on for almost four months, just a few days ago did the media start taking the news seriously and reporting it. This is because people are now noticing that most airplanes are not flying. The situation is getting worse, and now the United Nations has issued a statement saying that air transport will be halted completely as of next Monday."

"Why is this happening?"

"Every airplane is controlled by a computer system called the avionics, it is an essential element for every airplane because it allows the pilots to fly. Now, it is believed that there are a group of people who have found a way to hack this avionics system."

"But what happens if someone takes control of an aircraft computer system?"

"It's believed that the hackers can manipulate the aircraft's navigation system and change its flight path, or worse, hijack the planes remotely, like it happened last week on the Paris-London flight. No one knows yet what the group of terrorists wants, but it is known that they have already hijacked and crashed planes, and even bombed airports."

"So, we have to walk to Asia?"

"We have no choice, because air transport is no longer a viable option."

As they approached the main square of Ankara, they stopped by a small stall. The vendor was selling water and some sweet fruit drinks. Cale took a sip of the water, it was very cold, but it tasted a little strange.

"Is it safe to drink this water?" Han asked.

"Yes, the water here in Ankara is safe to drink and it's a good idea to keep yourself hydrated during these walks. If we don't find any water to drink, just take this water with you, it will help you along the way."

* * *

Walking and walking until the end of the day, Cale and his companions were exhausted. They had camped out in a meadow on the outskirts of Ankara when they heard a sound coming from the distance.

"Does anyone hear that sound?" Cale asked.

"Yes, it sounds like a train." Ahmet responded.

"But the train won't be leaving anytime soon, they will be sleeping for the night. Come on, let's go find a place to set up camp."

"I don't think we'll find a place to camp here, this is a military training area." Han said.

"The military can't stop us from camping here, it's just an empty field with a train track running through it. We can camp wherever we want."

As they approached the train they could feel the vibrations and the loud clattering of the train as it moved on the tracks.

"What do you think they are carrying?" Ahmet asked.

"I have no idea, but I wonder if it could be something that could help us with our journey."

The train passed by them, and the sound of the metal on the tracks became quieter, disappearing in the distance.

"Let's continue walking, it's getting cold." Cale said.

The night passed quickly and the day came faster than they thought. They packed their things and continued walking along the road to the city of Konya. Konya was a long way off, but they knew they needed to reach it to find out more about their journey.

* * *

Konya was a beautiful city with a rich history. As they walked through the streets, Cale could feel the energy of the city, a vibrant mix of old and new. Even if the city had been changed by the world events that were happening, it had a charm that could not be destroyed.

"What do you know about Konya?" Cale asked.

"Konya is the capital of the Turkish region, historically known for its connections with the arts and knowledge. The city is home to one of the most important mystics of the past century, Rumi, and has a temple dedicated to him. His teachings are still popular today." Ahmet replied.

"It's hard to believe that this city was the home of the great philosopher, Rumi, and now we are here living in fear, with no other option but to walk."

"I have heard that there are still some people who live in a rural area far from the city, where they have made a pact to live without technology. This place is called the 'Village of Silence', and maybe we can learn from them."

As they continued to walk through the city, they came across a bookstore with old books that were in excellent condition. The store's owner was a small woman with her hair in a bun and her glasses perched on the bridge of her nose.

"Are all these books old?" Cale asked.

"Yes, they are all ancient books. Some of them are thousands of years old."

"Do you know where we can find more information about this ‘Village of Silence’?"

"I can tell you that it is located about a day's walk from here, in the mountains, but I can't give you much more information, there are few people who still go there."

"Thank you, we'll be on our way." Cale said, as they started to head towards the mountains.

After leaving the city, they began to walk in a forest direction. The forest was beautiful, with trees that seemed to be reaching for the sky, and the air was fresh and cool. The woods were quiet, except for the constant noise of the wind.

"This is beautiful, let's set up camp here." Cale said, noticing the clearing in the trees.

The night was clear and the stars were shining bright in the sky, as they set up their camp, they felt a sense of peace.

* * *

The next day they continued to walk through the forest, when suddenly, two men appeared. One man was taller, with dark hair and a beard, the other man had blonde hair and a clean shaved face. The tall man spoke first.

"We are the 'Keepers of Silence', you came to our village looking for answers to your questions."

"That's right, we have been told that your village can help us."

"Follow us, we'll take you there."

They walked for about an hour, until they reached a small village nestled in the mountains. The village was surrounded by hills, with houses made of wood and stone, connected by small paths, which looked more like a fortified city.

"You are welcome here, take your rest. Tomorrow we will talk and I will give you the answers you seek." The tall man said as he nodded at Cale and his companions.

"Thank you, we'll be here." Cale replied.

The next day, the tall man gathered the travelers in a large room decorated with murals and ancient weapons. He sat down in a large chair in the center of the room and began to speak.

"We are the 'Keepers of Silence', you have come to us seeking answers, answers that we have been protecting for centuries. We have lived in this village for over one thousand years, and we have kept the fire of knowledge alive, even in the darkest times."

"We know that the world has changed, and that you have come here to try to understand why. We have been following the events that have been happening in the world and we are aware of the problems with airplanes. We know that there is a group of people who are hijacking planes and using them as weapons of terror. But what you do not know is that there is a way to prevent this from happening."

"What is this way?" Cale asked.

"It's simple, you need to cut off the airplanes' internet access and isolate them from the world. This way even if a group of people tries to hack the planes, they will not be able to do it. The problem is that the people who control the planes are the ones who can do this, but they are afraid to take this action because they fear that they will lose money."

"But if this is done, won't people suffer?"

"Yes, this will slow down the movement of people and it will cause economic problems, but in the long run this will protect the lives of many people. We, the 'Keepers of Silence', have decided to take a stand and we have isolated ourselves from the world. We have been living without technology for centuries, and we have seen how technology has led to ignorance, wars, and destruction. We hope that you will join us and help us to spread knowledge and to show the world that there is a way to live without technology."

"Thank you for your help, but we still have to reach Asia. We have to move on and continue our journey."

"We understand your situation, and we will help as much as we can. One of our members will travel with you and teach you the way of Silence. He will be your guide on your journey."

With that, a man with a long beard and a shaved head stepped forward, "I am Ziya, I will be your guide, and I will help you to follow the Silk Road."

* * *

Walking along the Silk Road with Ziya was an adventure. He was a man of few words

Question: If there were no more planes, how would you travel to another continent?
Answer: 

Cale looked at the other travelers, who were all staring at the same map, hanging on the wall of the airport with a sense of fear. The map was huge, it covered the entire north wall and was so detailed that you could pinpoint exactly where you were in the world.

"What continent do we want to go to?" Cale said with a frown.

"Asia, I think." Han, the Asian-looking traveler, stepped forward to answer.

"Oh, that's easy. Just follow the map."

"It's not just as easy as that anymore." Han looked back at Cale and shook his head. "Aren't you reading the news? A large part of the world's air transport network is shut down right now, planes are being stolen all over the world."

"The world? But what is going on exactly?"

"Do you remember the news report on the BBC World News about 'Hijackers in Planes'?"

"Oh, the one where they said a group of terrorists were controlling the passengers using a remote control that could hack and control aircraft computer systems?"

"Yes, the one that has created fear all over the world, turning every plane into a potential target."

Cale took a step back and looked around. This was not what he expected. He had arrived in Istanbul just over a week ago, only to find that the world had changed overnight. Now he was stuck with several other travelers with the goal of reaching Asia. What awaited them on the other side of the world was still a mystery, but there was no choice left but to set out regardless.

Han was speaking again, "We saw a group of travelers who said they made it to the mountains of Nepal and it is said that a group of people in Nepal are planning to set off on an expedition to Tibet."

"Tibet..." Cale repeated weakly, looking at the mountains on the huge map.

The mountains were close, the road passed through Turkey, then passed over the Caspian Sea, into Kazakhstan and then crossed the Hindu Kush range. In front of Cale and his companions, it seemed like a long and dangerous journey.

"Let's look for a way." Cale moved closer to the map, looking at the various roads and transportation routes available to them. "Let's start with the easiest transport option in the region, but it's a long journey."

"What do you have in mind?"

"We can start walking along the Trans-Anatolian railway or we can go overland and follow the Silk Road, it's almost the same path."

"But the Silk Road was used by the Chinese thousands of years ago, do they still use it?"

"It's still being used, even if only by a few, and there is even an ancient Chinese route that goes directly from Istanbul to Tibet."

"But this journey will take months, surely there's a different route?"

"If we use airplanes, of course there are other routes, but now that's not an option."

"We have no choice, let's leave for Ankara, we can find something in Ankara."

With that decision made, they set off with their backpacks towards the capital city of Turkey, Ankara, the first stop on their journey.

* * *

Walking along the streets of Ankara, Cale felt a strange sensation, as if the earth were breathing, the rhythm of the street seemed to pulse. As he walked with his traveler companions, he found it increasingly difficult to believe that it was this very city that was causing the world's air transport network to shrink.

"What are those buildings?" Cale asked, pointing at a group of large buildings.

"Those are the Turkish Airlines Headquarters, this one looks like a spaceship." Ahmet, one of Cale's companions, explained.

"Is it true that they have been closed for months? Why can't they fly now?"

"Yes, they have been closed for months. It all started when some terrorists took over three Turkish Airlines planes at the beginning of October. Two were hijacked at the Istanbul airport while the third was hijacked over the Black Sea."

"That was in October, but we just found out a few days ago that planes are being hijacked all over the world, how did that happen?"

"This has been going on for almost four months, just a few days ago did the media start taking the news seriously and reporting it. This is because people are now noticing that most airplanes are not flying. The situation is getting worse, and now the United Nations has issued a statement saying that air transport will be halted completely as of next Monday."

"Why is this happening?"

"Every airplane is controlled by a computer system called the avionics, it is an essential element for every airplane because it allows the pilots to fly. Now, it is believed that there are a group of people who have found a way to hack this avionics system."

"But what happens if someone takes control of an aircraft computer system?"

"It's believed that the hackers can manipulate the aircraft's navigation system and change its flight path, or worse, hijack the planes remotely, like it happened last week on the Paris-London flight. No one knows yet what the group of terrorists wants, but it is known that they have already hijacked and crashed planes, and even bombed airports."

"So, we have to walk to Asia?"

"We have no choice, because air transport is no longer a viable option."

As they approached the main square of Ankara, they stopped by a small stall. The vendor was selling water and some sweet fruit drinks. Cale took a sip of the water, it was very cold, but it tasted a little strange.

"Is it safe to drink this water?" Han asked.

"Yes, the water here in Ankara is safe to drink and it's a good idea to keep yourself hydrated during these walks. If we don't find any water to drink, just take this water with you, it will help you along the way."

* * *

Walking and walking until the end of the day, Cale and his companions were exhausted. They had camped out in a meadow on the outskirts of Ankara when they heard a sound coming from the distance.

"Does anyone hear that sound?" Cale asked.

"Yes, it sounds like a train." Ahmet responded.

"But the train won't be leaving anytime soon, they will be sleeping for the night. Come on, let's go find a place to set up camp."

"I don't think we'll find a place to camp here, this is a military training area." Han said.

"The military can't stop us from camping here, it's just an empty field with a train track running through it. We can camp wherever we want."

As they approached the train they could feel the vibrations and the loud clattering of the train as it moved on the tracks.

"What do you think they are carrying?" Ahmet asked.

"I have no idea, but I wonder if it could be something that could help us with our journey."

The train passed by them, and the sound of the metal on the tracks became quieter, disappearing in the distance.

"Let's continue walking, it's getting cold." Cale said.

The night passed quickly and the day came faster than they thought. They packed their things and continued walking along the road to the city of Konya. Konya was a long way off, but they knew they needed to reach it to find out more about their journey.

* * *

Konya was a beautiful city with a rich history. As they walked through the streets, Cale could feel the energy of the city, a vibrant mix of old and new. Even if the city had been changed by the world events that were happening, it had a charm that could not be destroyed.

"What do you know about Konya?" Cale asked.

"Konya is the capital of the Turkish region, historically known for its connections with the arts and knowledge. The city is home to one of the most important mystics of the past century, Rumi, and has a temple dedicated to him. His teachings are still popular today." Ahmet replied.

"It's hard to believe that this city was the home of the great philosopher, Rumi, and now we are here living in fear, with no other option but to walk."

"I have heard that there are still some people who live in a rural area far from the city, where they have made a pact to live without technology. This place is called the 'Village of Silence', and maybe we can learn from them."

As they continued to walk through the city, they came across a bookstore with old books that were in excellent condition. The store's owner was a small woman with her hair in a bun and her glasses perched on the bridge of her nose.

"Are all these books old?" Cale asked.

"Yes, they are all ancient books. Some of them are thousands of years old."

"Do you know where we can find more information about this ‘Village of Silence’?"

"I can tell you that it is located about a day's walk from here, in the mountains, but I can't give you much more information, there are few people who still go there."

"Thank you, we'll be on our way." Cale said, as they started to head towards the mountains.

After leaving the city, they began to walk in a forest direction. The forest was beautiful, with trees that seemed to be reaching for the sky, and the air was fresh and cool. The woods were quiet, except for the constant noise of the wind.

"This is beautiful, let's set up camp here." Cale said, noticing the clearing in the trees.

The night was clear and the stars were shining bright in the sky, as they set up their camp, they felt a sense of peace.

* * *

The next day they continued to walk through the forest, when suddenly, two men appeared. One man was taller, with dark hair and a beard, the other man had blonde hair and a clean shaved face. The tall man spoke first.

"We are the 'Keepers of Silence', you came to our village looking for answers to your questions."

"That's right, we have been told that your village can help us."

"Follow us, we'll take you there."

They walked for about an hour, until they reached a small village nestled in the mountains. The village was surrounded by hills, with houses made of wood and stone, connected by small paths, which looked more like a fortified city.

"You are welcome here, take your rest. Tomorrow we will talk and I will give you the answers you seek." The tall man said as he nodded at Cale and his companions.

"Thank you, we'll be here." Cale replied.

The next day, the tall man gathered the travelers in a large room decorated with murals and ancient weapons. He sat down in a large chair in the center of the room and began to speak.

"We are the 'Keepers of Silence', you have come to us seeking answers, answers that we have been protecting for centuries. We have lived in this village for over one thousand years, and we have kept the fire of knowledge alive, even in the darkest times."

"We know that the world has changed, and that you have come here to try to understand why. We have been following the events that have been happening in the world and we are aware of the problems with airplanes. We know that there is a group of people who are hijacking planes and using them as weapons of terror. But what you do not know is that there is a way to prevent this from happening."

"What is this way?" Cale asked.

"It's simple, you need to cut off the airplanes' internet access and isolate them from the world. This way even if a group of people tries to hack the planes, they will not be able to do it. The problem is that the people who control the planes are the ones who can do this, but they are afraid to take this action because they fear that they will lose money."

"But if this is done, won't people suffer?"

"Yes, this will slow down the movement of people and it will cause economic problems, but in the long run this will protect the lives of many people. We, the 'Keepers of Silence', have decided to take a stand and we have isolated ourselves from the world. We have been living without technology for centuries, and we have seen how technology has led to ignorance, wars, and destruction. We hope that you will join us and help us to spread knowledge and to show the world that there is a way to live without technology."

"Thank you for your help, but we still have to reach Asia. We have to move on and continue our journey."

"We understand your situation, and we will help as much as we can. One of our members will travel with you and teach you the way of Silence. He will be your guide on your journey."

With that, a man with a long beard and a shaved head stepped forward, "I am Ziya, I will be your guide, and I will help you to follow the Silk Road."

* * *

Walking along the Silk Road with Ziya was an adventure. He was a man of few words

This network can serve as an alternative transportation system, giving you options and making your town or city more pedestrian- and bike-friendly.

This network is the "parks-for-transport" concept, which is aimed at enhancing the quality of life in urban settings. It goes beyond recreation and offers a greener alternative for commuting.

Aside from the benefits of parks being the key to alternative transportation, it also provides a multitude of health benefits and promotes sustainability.

## The Health Benefits of Spending Time in Parks

While everyone loves summer, the heat can sometimes become too unbearable, giving you an excuse to skip out on exercise. However, did you know that not getting regular physical activity can lead to a variety of health problems?

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), physical inactivity ranks fourth as a risk factor for global mortality, causing an estimated 3.2 million deaths each year.

Not getting enough exercise can lead to health issues like obesity, heart disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes. It also increases the risks of developing certain types of cancer and mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, and dementia.

But what if you live in a city with endless traffic, high levels of air pollution, or areas where it's not safe to walk?

Fortunately, researchers have proposed that incorporating parks into commuting solutions can help improve your health and fitness.

### Reducing the Burden of Chronic Diseases

A study published in BMJ Open identified a key component of urban design that contributes to people's health: the built environment. The researchers mentioned parks as an essential feature of an urban landscape that promotes physical activity.

People who live in an area with parks have an increased likelihood of being active, getting enough exercise, and reducing their risk of obesity and chronic diseases.

### Lowering Stress Levels

Exercising in a green space like a park isn't just good for your body; it's also beneficial for your mind. A study in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health found that exercise in a natural environment — including parks — can help reduce stress and enhance the mental health of women.

A similar study in Nature showed that even brief encounters with nature, like going for a walk in a park, can help lower stress levels and improve emotional well-being.

## Promoting Sustainability Through Green Transport

Commuting through green transport means choosing sustainable and environmentally friendly modes of transportation. In an ideal world, we'd all be walking or biking to work, which would significantly reduce carbon emissions.

However, this isn't always possible, especially if you live in an area where it's not safe to walk or bike to work. But with the establishment of parks-for-transport networks, you might find it easier to commute sustainably.

### Encouraging Active Commuting

While many people would choose cars over walking or biking, others may be more hesitant due to safety concerns. One way to ease people into the active commuting lifestyle is by building safe paths through parks.

Parks-for-transport networks can connect residential areas with schools, offices, and other important facilities, encouraging people to leave their cars at home and walk or bike instead.

### Reducing Carbon Emissions

According to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), transportation is the leading contributor to U.S. greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, accounting for 29% of total U.S. GHG emissions in 2020. This massive contribution is primarily due to the use of fossil fuels in cars and other vehicles.

By using parks for commuting, we can reduce our carbon footprint and minimize the number of cars on the road. Doing so would help lower GHG emissions and contribute to the global fight against climate change.

## Creating Greener and Healthier Cities

A parks-for-transport network may seem like an unusual idea, but it's a promising concept that can provide a multitude of benefits for both individuals and communities.

Encouraging active commuting and promoting sustainable transportation can go a long way in encouraging us to live healthier and more eco-conscious lives.

If your city doesn't have a parks-for-transport system yet, maybe it's time to propose the idea to your local government. A greener and healthier city is just a vote away.

This could become a problem in the future as our planet heats up and resources become scarcer. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have taken important steps to develop a lens-free retinal implant that could improve the vision of people with degenerative diseases that affect the photoreceptors of the eye.

The researchers presented their findings at the annual meeting of the Optical Society (OSA) in San Francisco in July. In their experiments, they demonstrated that the implant, which consists of a miniaturized micro-electromechanical system (MEMS), could potentially restore vision in patients with degenerative diseases of the retina, such as retinitis pigmentosa or age-related macular degeneration.

"These [diseases] attack the photoreceptor cells," said Ebrahim Izadpanah at the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at Berkeley, the lead author of the study. "So far there is no effective treatment for these conditions, other than the Argus II retinal prosthesis," he continued. The Argus II, also known as the "bionic eye," is the first retinal implant approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of retinitis pigmentosa patients.

Izadpanah and his colleagues argue that while the Argus II has been successful in restoring some useful vision to patients, it has some limitations. In particular, it is not able to restore the sensitivity of the normal retina and its resolution, leaving patients with a "grainy" vision. Also, the Argus II implant requires glasses to be worn, since it cannot compensate for high or low contrast in images.

To overcome these limitations, the team has developed a lens-free device that combines photodetectors, a digital signal processor and an electronic stimulation system to electrically stimulate the optic nerve and directly restore image perception. The device is based on a microfluidic silicon chip called OCTAX, which creates an accurate three-dimensional image of the scene.

"The device we've built takes advantage of the complex geometry of a MEMS structure to create an image without using a lens," said Izadpanah. This new device can capture images that are far sharper than those taken directly by the Argus II. The team used this technology to record videos of images viewed under a variety of stimuli, including dim and overexposed conditions.

"What makes this work unique and a significant advance in retinal prosthetics is the combination of a lens-free retina, which reduces the number of elements of the implant and achieves a higher resolution compared to the Argus II, with artificial intelligence to allow the device to function in different lighting conditions," said Izadpanah.

The team also conducted a retinal implant simulation to estimate the time frame of the device's development. Answer:  This could become a problem in the future as our planet heats up and resources become scarcer. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have taken important steps to develop a lens-free retinal implant that could improve the vision of people with degenerative diseases that affect the photoreceptors of the eye.

The researchers presented their findings at the annual meeting of the Optical Society (OSA) in San Francisco in July. In their experiments, they demonstrated that the implant, which consists of a miniaturized micro-electromechanical system (MEMS), could potentially restore vision in patients with degenerative diseases of the retina, such as retinitis pigmentosa or age-related macular degeneration.

"These [diseases] attack the photoreceptor cells," said Ebrahim Izadpanah at the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at Berkeley, the lead author of the study. "So far there is no effective treatment for these conditions, other than the Argus II retinal prosthesis," he continued. The Argus II, also known as the "bionic eye," is the first retinal implant approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of retinitis pigmentosa patients.

Izadpanah and his colleagues argue that while the Argus II has been successful in restoring some useful vision to patients, it has some limitations. In particular, it is not able to restore the sensitivity of the normal retina and its resolution, leaving patients with a "grainy" vision. Also, the Argus II implant requires glasses to be worn, since it cannot compensate for high or low contrast in images.

To overcome these limitations, the team has developed a lens-free device that combines photodetectors, a digital signal processor and an electronic stimulation system to electrically stimulate the optic nerve and directly restore image perception. The device is based on a microfluidic silicon chip called OCTAX, which creates an accurate three-dimensional image of the scene.

"The device we've built takes advantage of the complex geometry of a MEMS structure to create an image without using a lens," said Izadpanah. This new device can capture images that are far sharper than those taken directly by the Argus II. The team used this technology to record videos of images viewed under a variety of stimuli, including dim and overexposed conditions.

"What makes this work unique and a significant advance in retinal prosthetics is the combination of a lens-free retina, which reduces the number of elements of the implant and achieves a higher resolution compared to the Argus II, with artificial intelligence to allow the device to function in different lighting conditions," said Izadpanah.

The team also conducted a retinal implant simulation to estimate the time frame of the device's development. "Based on our simulations, the lens-free retinal implant technology is at least 10 years away from being used for treating retinal degenerative diseases," said study co-author and research scientist Ali Khodadadzadeh. Yet the technology, if developed, could potentially provide patients with natural and sharp images that they can perceive without glasses or contact lenses.

6. **Adaptation**: Some people might learn to adapt to their new visual reality, using other senses more, and developing new ways to navigate and communicate. For example, they might learn braille or use voice recognition software.

7. **Social Interaction**: Sight is a significant part of social interaction. People might feel isolated due to not being able to see their loved ones or friends.

8. **Access to Medical Care**: People with poor vision might have difficulty accessing medical care if they can't read directions or understand what a doctor is saying.

In conclusion, if all glasses and contact lenses disappeared, life would become much more difficult for people with poor vision, affecting many aspects of their lives. It's a testament to the importance of vision care and the technology that allows us to correct vision impairments.

output.text_basic:
Without guidance, you'd likely rely on landmarks and familiar sights to get to your destination. In our physical world, landmarks like the Eiffel Tower and Golden Gate Bridge are easy to spot, but the same can't always be said for virtual spaces.

In the digital world, you need digital landmarks to navigate with accuracy and confidence. These landmarks don't replace the need for physical signs and systems, but rather help to create a consistent, easy-to-understand context in digital spaces.

## Landmarks in Digital Spaces

"Digital landmarks" are visible elements within user interfaces that clearly define different sections or components. These features help users navigate a digital environment more easily and complete tasks with greater efficiency.

In an application, they help users find and navigate areas by using familiar symbols, images, or text. While their utility is clear, digital landmarks serve additional purposes beyond simple navigation, including:

1. Signaling action - A digital landmark provides a clear indication of what to do in a given space. For example, a "sign in" button shows users where they can enter their credentials.

2. Delivering context - Digital landmarks deliver information about what users can expect to see or do in a particular area, like the shopping cart or search function.

3. Adding meaning - Landmarks give structure to a user interface. They add context, making it easier for users to understand the application and its features.

4. Building familiarity - By using consistent digital landmarks, developers can create more familiar and comfortable user experiences for their audiences. Users intuitively understand and remember where to find certain features when they visit a digital space again.

5. Facilitating accessibility - Digital landmarks can help make user interfaces more accessible by providing additional context to users with disabilities or low-context processing skills.

## Examples of Digital Landmarks

Digital landmarks exist in various forms across countless digital spaces. Here are a few examples:

1. Navigation bars - Top bars on websites and apps containing menus, search fields, and user avatars.

2. Hamburger menus - Three horizontal lines that, when clicked, open up a side menu containing links to various sections. This type of menu is particularly useful in mobile applications.

3. Call-to-action buttons - Big, prominent buttons that initiate actions, like “Sign Up” or “Download Now.” They clearly signal what users need to do to progress through the application.

4. Breadcrumbs - Navigation elements that represent the user's current location within a multi-level site structure, like "Home > Shop > Electronics > Headphones."

5. Page headers - Titles that denote the name and context of the current screen.

6. Icons - Simple visual symbols that represent features, functions, or actions. For example, a download icon typically resembles a downward-pointing arrow.

7. Folders - Visible containers in file management systems that store files or other folders.

8. Application windows - Separate windows or tabs within an application that represent different features or modules.

While every digital space is unique, the principles behind digital landmarks hold steadfast. Providing intuitive and predictable navigation elements enhances the overall user experience and encourages more frequent, positive interactions with your brand.

## How to Create Useful Digital Landmarks

When designing digital landmarks, keep the following principles in mind:

1. Keep it Simple: Avoid using overly complex or ambiguous icons that may confuse users.

2. Be Consistent: Use the same symbols and labels across your application to create familiarity and make navigation easier for users.

3. Offer Context: Make sure each digital landmark offers context about its purpose or function. This helps users understand the purpose behind each component and make more informed decisions about where to navigate.

4. Prioritize Importance: Differentiate between different digital landmarks according to their importance. Use visual cues, like size, color, or prominence, to distinguish one from another.

5. Test and Refine: Incorporate user testing to improve the effectiveness of your digital landmarks. Gather feedback on the clarity, intuitiveness, and effectiveness of each landmark, and use it to refine your design.

6. Accessibility Guidelines: Ensure your digital landmarks are accessible to all users, including those with disabilities. Use alt text for visual elements, maintain a consistent color palette, and consider whether the landmarks are easily operable via assistive technology.

By incorporating these principles into your digital landmark design, you will create an intuitive, enjoyable, and accessible experience for your users.

## Final Thoughts

Digital landmarks enable users to navigate digital spaces more effectively, thereby enhancing their overall experience and fostering a stronger connection with the brand. By incorporating digital landmarks thoughtfully, developers can make sophisticated, complex platforms accessible and engaging for more users.

For the most successful results, create digital landmarks that are visually unique, easily recognizable, and offer context to users. Don’t be afraid to iterate upon your landmarks based on user feedback and testing. Continuously refining your design will ensure that your digital spaces remain intuitive, accessible, and enjoyable for all users.

1. Follow the sun: Since the sun always rises in the east and sets in the west, you could navigate by following the sun during the day and the stars at night. This technique, while not the fastest, has been used by early explorers and nomadic tribes for thousands of years.

2. Memorize landmarks: If you are traveling through a relatively familiar area or one with distinct landmarks, you could potentially memorize key features and use them to guide your way.

3. Ask for directions: Human interaction might still be an option, even without maps or technology. You could ask locals or travelers for directions, providing you can communicate effectively.

4. Follow rivers and coastlines: Both rivers and coastlines offer a sense of direction and often lead to cities, which can provide help and navigation tools.

5. Use native plants and animals: Some plants and animals have unique characteristics or behaviors that can help with navigation. For example, monarch butterflies follow a specific migratory path, or some plants grow in specific soil conditions.

6. Build a compass: By creating a makeshift compass using minerals like magnetite, lodestone, or even cobalt, you could navigate using the magnetic fields of the Earth.

7. Use the wind: Wind patterns can be an indicator of direction, and you can learn to interpret these patterns based on your environment.

8. Navigate by smell: Certain smells can be associated with specific directions or locations. For example, the ocean might have a distinct salty smell, while forests can have a distinct aroma due to the trees and vegetation.

9. Use the moon: The moon has a constant cycle and rises roughly 12 hours after the sun (at a different location, of course). By observing the moon's position, you could potentially find your way.

10. Create your own map: If you have time, you could create your own map using natural markers, such as trees, rocks, or landmarks. You could then follow this map on your journey.

11. Follow animal migration paths: Certain animals migrate along specific routes, such as birds flying south for the winter or mammals following seasonal food sources. By observing these animals, you could potentially find your way.

12. Use natural timekeepers: Some plants and animals have predictable life cycles that can serve as natural timekeepers. For example, flowers might bloom at specific times of the year, or migratory birds might pass through at certain months. By observing these patterns, you could potentially track the passage of time and plan your journey accordingly.

13. Use sound: Some sounds, such as the distant rumble of a waterfall or the chirping of a specific bird species, can serve as indicators of direction.

14. Follow the horizon: By observing the horizon, you can determine which direction is north (assuming you have some prior knowledge or can find a compass or a lodestone). From there, you can follow the compass heading using your surroundings.

15. Create a makeshift boat: If you find yourself near a body of water, you could potentially build a makeshift boat using materials like driftwood, vines, and animal hides. This would allow you to travel faster and cover more ground while still relying on natural navigation methods like following rivers and coastlines.

The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. So if you're standing somewhere and the sun rose from that direction, it must be behind you now and in front of you is the west.

So your first step is to head west. This will get you closer to the place you come from, but it's better than nothing.

Now, if you find a body of water, like a river or a lake, it usually flows to a large source, like an ocean. If you follow the river or the lake's shoreline or, if possible, the river itself, it should lead you to the ocean. If there are cities along the way, they're usually located near large bodies of water, so you might find one and ask for help.

If there are no bodies of water, look for mountains or hills. They're usually the highest points in the area and offer a better view. Climbing a hill or a mountain may help you spot other landmarks, rivers, or cities that could guide you.

If you find a path or road, follow it. If it's going away from a river or a city, it might lead to another one. If it's very far, it might be a highway leading to a distant city.

Remember, the stars can help you at night. The North Star (Polaris) can show you North. So if you find it, you can figure out which direction you should go.

If you have a compass or a watch that tells the time zone, you can use it to find which direction is north.

You can also look for migratory birds to help you. They usually travel north in the spring and south in the fall. If you find a bird you suspect is migratory, observe its direction and head the same way.

Lastly, if you're lost in a forest, make loud noises or light a fire. Rescue teams look for such signs when searching for lost people.

This is a very basic guide and won't work in all situations. But it's a start. And remember, it's always better to be prepared. Always carry a map, a compass, a whistle, and a light source with you.
