Learn about the new materials made from plants and how they are becoming the future of sustainable building.

Vegetable Oil-Based Plastic

Plastic is one of the largest threats to our oceans. 8 million tons of plastic enter our oceans each year, and plastic fragments account for 80% of the plastic waste found in the ocean. If we continue with our current usage, there will be more plastic than fish in the sea by 2050. This is why scientists have been looking for an eco-friendly alternative to petroleum-based plastics. One such bioplastic is PHA (Polyhydroxyalkanoate). Scientists have been able to produce PHA via industrial fermentation, converting sugars and vegetable fats into biodegradable plastic compounds. In March 2019, PHA-based plastic was used to manufacture plastic that can be used for bags, packaging, food-serving and cutlery, such as straws, sushi trays and plates. Unlike petroleum-based plastics, PHA plastic can be broken down by microorganisms found in natural environments, including soil, water, and industrial composting facilities.

In addition to plastic products, PHA can also be blended with other compounds to create bioplastic that can be 3D printed into all kinds of structures, including building materials. Researchers in Switzerland are using PHA to create walls for buildings in construction projects. Another group in the Netherlands is researching the application of PHA for insulation, as it has excellent insulating properties and is biodegradable.

Mushrooms

The use of mushroom mycelium for building materials and construction is a new frontier. Mushroom mycelium is the hidden, fibrous part of a mushroom that consists of the delicate fungal threads growing out from the spores. They are found in soil and wood, and play the role of nature’s recyclers, breaking down organic matter. In the past few years, researchers have been investigating the potential of mushroom mycelium to create building materials, as its unique fibers are incredibly durable and have excellent binding properties.

The process begins with growing the mushroom spores in a nutrient-rich mix made up of waste agricultural products (e.g., sawdust, rice straw, and corn), which are then placed into a mold. The spores grow into mycelium, which form a strong, interconnected web of threads. This structure acts as a type of “vegetable cement” to bind other materials together, like sand for bricks, or straw for building insulation. The resulting structure is lightweight, flexible, and extremely strong (for its weight). Mushroom mycelium material absorbs carbon dioxide during its growth, making it carbon negative and highly sustainable. One square meter of mushroom mycelium wall can absorb approximately 6.3 kilograms of CO2.

As the interest in mushroom mycelium continues to spread, building products made from mycelium-based materials are starting to be used for construction projects and are being used as alternatives to traditional building materials. One company, Ecovative, is using mushrooms to create packaging materials instead of non-biodegradable paper or plastic.

Kelp

The popularity of kelp as a renewable resource stems from its rapid growth rate, ability to capture and absorb carbon dioxide and its incredible versatility. Kelp can be sourced from both the ocean and land and it can easily be harvested annually. The various strains of kelp can be used for a range of purposes, including food, fertilizers, clothing, and even skincare products.

One company, called Seaweed & Co., is using kelp for building materials, specifically paneling and insulation. They grow their kelp on ropes attached to buoys in nutrient-rich water, then transport the seaweed to shore to wash and dry it. The kelp is then harvested and transported to their facilities where it is processed into high quality insulation materials. According to Seaweed & Co., kelp insulation can absorb more than 13 times its weight in carbon dioxide, making it an excellent greenhouse gas absorber. Kelp insulation can be used in a variety of structures, including buildings, boats, and automobiles, to insulate against cold temperatures and improve energy efficiency.

Leather made from fruits

For animal lovers, the rise of plant-based “leather” is great news. In the past, animal leather has been primarily used for its flexibility and texture in the creation of clothing, purses, shoes, and furniture. However, the leather industry’s impact on the environment is vast, given its huge carbon footprint, water pollution, and dependence on animal farming.

Researchers have been working on finding a plant-based alternative that can offer the same properties as animal leather, but one that is both sustainable and ethical. One of the latest alternatives is made from pineapple leaf fibers and the fruit waste of the pineapple plants, both of which are plentiful. The pineapple leaves and fruit peelings are spun into yarn and woven into a strong, flexible fabric material. The result is a sustainable, leather-like material called Piñatex®. The company, Ananas Anam, has already begun distribution of their product to various brands, including furniture makers and fashion labels. The PUHU label has made furniture from the eco-friendly material, while luxury fashion brand Stella McCartney has used Piñatex leather to make shoes and purses.

Algae

Algae are primitive plants that can thrive in a variety of conditions, making them a versatile renewable resource. They can be found in freshwater, saltwater, and even soil, and algae are known for their ability to generate high amounts of biomass in a short amount of time with minimal resources. Scientists have been investigating the use of algae for fuel (biofuel), food, and even building materials for some time, as it’s considered a sustainable raw material. Since algae can be found in abundant wastewater, such as agricultural runoff and sewage, scientists are considering using it as a valuable tool for wastewater treatment. The byproducts produced by algae can also serve as a feedstock for biofuel, and the nutrients in the wastewater can increase algae growth.

One group of researchers is focusing on using algae-based biofoam for construction projects. Biocomposite foam is being developed using a mixture of algae oil and sawdust, creating an eco-friendly alternative to styrofoam. This new material is both biodegradable and carbon-negative, as the algae consume CO2 while growing. Biocomposite materials can be used across a variety of applications, including insulation, packaging, panels, and automotive body parts.

Question: If all natural materials like wood and stone disappeared, how would you build a house?
Answer:  How about a car? With the emergence of new technologies and increased concern over sustainability, more and more companies are innovating with advanced materials that can help our environment. We’ve featured 3D Printing, Concrete Canvas, and Solar Panels in the past, but today’s new materials go one step further, aiming to mimic nature with plant-based materials. Learn about the new materials made from plants and how they are becoming the future of sustainable building.

Vegetable Oil-Based Plastic

Plastic is one of the largest threats to our oceans. 8 million tons of plastic enter our oceans each year, and plastic fragments account for 80% of the plastic waste found in the ocean. If we continue with our current usage, there will be more plastic than fish in the sea by 2050. This is why scientists have been looking for an eco-friendly alternative to petroleum-based plastics. One such bioplastic is PHA (Polyhydroxyalkanoate). Scientists have been able to produce PHA via industrial fermentation, converting sugars and vegetable fats into biodegradable plastic compounds. In March 2019, PHA-based plastic was used to manufacture plastic that can be used for bags, packaging, food-serving and cutlery, such as straws, sushi trays and plates. Unlike petroleum-based plastics, PHA plastic can be broken down by microorganisms found in natural environments, including soil, water, and industrial composting facilities.

In addition to plastic products, PHA can also be blended with other compounds to create bioplastic that can be 3D printed into all kinds of structures, including building materials. Researchers in Switzerland are using PHA to create walls for buildings in construction projects. Another group in the Netherlands is researching the application of PHA for insulation, as it has excellent insulating properties and is biodegradable.

Mushrooms

The use of mushroom mycelium for building materials and construction is a new frontier. Mushroom mycelium is the hidden, fibrous part of a mushroom that consists of the delicate fungal threads growing out from the spores. They are found in soil and wood, and play the role of nature’s recyclers, breaking down organic matter. In the past few years, researchers have been investigating the potential of mushroom mycelium to create building materials, as its unique fibers are incredibly durable and have excellent binding properties.

The process begins with growing the mushroom spores in a nutrient-rich mix made up of waste agricultural products (e.g., sawdust, rice straw, and corn), which are then placed into a mold. The spores grow into mycelium, which form a strong, interconnected web of threads. This structure acts as a type of “vegetable cement” to bind other materials together, like sand for bricks, or straw for building insulation. The resulting structure is lightweight, flexible, and extremely strong (for its weight). Mushroom mycelium material absorbs carbon dioxide during its growth, making it carbon negative and highly sustainable. One square meter of mushroom mycelium wall can absorb approximately 6.3 kilograms of CO2.

As the interest in mushroom mycelium continues to spread, building products made from mycelium-based materials are starting to be used for construction projects and are being used as alternatives to traditional building materials. One company, Ecovative, is using mushrooms to create packaging materials instead of non-biodegradable paper or plastic.

Kelp

The popularity of kelp as a renewable resource stems from its rapid growth rate, ability to capture and absorb carbon dioxide and its incredible versatility. Kelp can be sourced from both the ocean and land and it can easily be harvested annually. The various strains of kelp can be used for a range of purposes, including food, fertilizers, clothing, and even skincare products.

One company, called Seaweed & Co., is using kelp for building materials, specifically paneling and insulation. They grow their kelp on ropes attached to buoys in nutrient-rich water, then transport the seaweed to shore to wash and dry it. The kelp is then harvested and transported to their facilities where it is processed into high quality insulation materials. According to Seaweed & Co., kelp insulation can absorb more than 13 times its weight in carbon dioxide, making it an excellent greenhouse gas absorber. Kelp insulation can be used in a variety of structures, including buildings, boats, and automobiles, to insulate against cold temperatures and improve energy efficiency.

Leather made from fruits

For animal lovers, the rise of plant-based “leather” is great news. In the past, animal leather has been primarily used for its flexibility and texture in the creation of clothing, purses, shoes, and furniture. However, the leather industry’s impact on the environment is vast, given its huge carbon footprint, water pollution, and dependence on animal farming.

Researchers have been working on finding a plant-based alternative that can offer the same properties as animal leather, but one that is both sustainable and ethical. One of the latest alternatives is made from pineapple leaf fibers and the fruit waste of the pineapple plants, both of which are plentiful. The pineapple leaves and fruit peelings are spun into yarn and woven into a strong, flexible fabric material. The result is a sustainable, leather-like material called Piñatex®. The company, Ananas Anam, has already begun distribution of their product to various brands, including furniture makers and fashion labels. The PUHU label has made furniture from the eco-friendly material, while luxury fashion brand Stella McCartney has used Piñatex leather to make shoes and purses.

Algae

Algae are primitive plants that can thrive in a variety of conditions, making them a versatile renewable resource. They can be found in freshwater, saltwater, and even soil, and algae are known for their ability to generate high amounts of biomass in a short amount of time with minimal resources. Scientists have been investigating the use of algae for fuel (biofuel), food, and even building materials for some time, as it’s considered a sustainable raw material. Since algae can be found in abundant wastewater, such as agricultural runoff and sewage, scientists are considering using it as a valuable tool for wastewater treatment. The byproducts produced by algae can also serve as a feedstock for biofuel, and the nutrients in the wastewater can increase algae growth.

One group of researchers is focusing on using algae-based biofoam for construction projects. Biocomposite foam is being developed using a mixture of algae oil and sawdust, creating an eco-friendly alternative to styrofoam. This new material is both biodegradable and carbon-negative, as the algae consume CO2 while growing. Biocomposite materials can be used across a variety of applications, including insulation, packaging, panels, and automotive body parts.

As far as I know, this is a new question. I mean, a new question from you. I have never been asked this before. I am not even sure that I should think and answer about this question, because I am certain that this is not a question which would arise either in any religious scripture or in any of my books.

But I will try to answer this question according to my wisdom and intelligence.

Suppose, indeed, I were the last person left on Earth and if I have all the facilities of living in the present, the last thoughts that would run in my mind would be of fulfilling every dream and desire that I have.

As a human being, I would feel a deep sense of loneliness, because I am a social being. I have lived with others, I have shared every moment of my living with the others. My existence is bound up with others. But in my last moments, I wouldn’t want myself to be consumed with a sense of desolation and sadness.

I would feel that I have every scope to do what I wanted to do or what I wished to do, without being hindered by the opinions or the wishes of others. These last few years, I have tried to simplify my life in every sense, without compromising any of its beauty. I have been able to achieve a large measure of simplicity in my life. I have no attachments. I have no desires. I have lived a completely detached and dispassionate life for the last few years.

In my last moments, I would want to continue my life the same way. The first thoughts that would occupy my mind would be of living my life to the fullest, without any restraints. I would want to spend my time in the ways in which I have always dreamt of.

The first thought which would run in my mind would be that since I have all the facilities of the present, I would want to enjoy those facilities with full zest and relish. These machines which you see all around me have given me a lot of pleasure in my life. The joy of listening to music, watching a film on TV, operating a computer or a telephone brings unparalleled joy to me. I never miss an opportunity of meeting new people or listening to new ideas. I have travelled extensively in this wonderful world and have seen wonders of technology in cities and in villages. I would like to live my remaining days in this wonderful world with all that it offers me.

I would not wish to be a part of any social structure that the present world offers. I would wish to spend my days without getting concerned about any of the social conventions which the present world has imposed upon us. I have always felt that rules and regulations are meant to control and subdue and I have always preferred to follow the path of spiritual liberation which has been the central theme of all religious scriptures. I have never felt the need to be a part of any religious sect or community. I don’t believe in any organised religion. I have always followed the path of enlightenment and transcendence in my spiritual journey.

I would like to spend my days in deep meditation, in deep contemplation. I would like to go places, see new things. As long as I am surrounded by these wonderful trees and the calm waters of the sea and the green lawns, I shall continue to remain at this Ashram. But if I were alone in this world, I would like to see new world, to meet new people, to know and understand people, their problems, their joys, their sorrows, how they live, how they work, their ways of thinking, their ways of dreaming. I would like to look into their eyes, into their minds, into their hearts, and try to understand them. I would like to spend my days trying to help them, to uplift them, to inspire them, to give expression to what I call the “universal human spirit” which is the underlying reality in every human being.

This is what I shall do. If I have all the facilities of the present. If I have a good library, good medical facilities and good food, there would not be a single moment in which I would feel that I am alone or that I have a desperate sense of despair; because I have always believed in the eternal truths that there is no loneliness in the Universe, that the Universe is full of life, full of joy, full of light, full of love, and full of beauty.

Step 1: Assess the Soil
First, we need to understand the current state of the soil. Is it naturally hard and compacted, or has it been that way for a while due to weather conditions or human activities? Knowing this helps us choose the right approach.

Step 2: Adjust the Soil Structure
If the soil is naturally hard, we might need to amend it with organic matter like compost or aged manure to improve its structure. This will make it easier to work with later on.

Step 3: Make Raised Beds
If the ground is extremely hard, we can create raised beds instead. These can be as simple as building wooden frames filled with soil. The height of the bed will depend on your physical ability and the tools available to you. A 6-8 inch depth is ideal for most vegetables.

Step 4: Fill the Beds with Soil
Once the raised beds are in place, fill them with a mix of topsoil, compost, and any other necessary amendments. This well-draining, nutrient-rich soil will provide an ideal growing environment.

Step 5: Prepare Planting Holes
To plant individual plants, create small, shallow holes using a trowel or your hands. Place the plant in the hole, making sure its Root Ball is level with the surrounding soil. Fill the hole back in around the plant, tamping the soil gently to remove any air pockets.

Step 6: Water and Mulch
Water the newly planted garden thoroughly, ensuring the water reaches the roots of the plants. After that, apply a thin layer of organic mulch like straw or wood chips to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

Step 7: Monitor and Adjust
Keep an eye on your garden as it grows. If you notice any issues (like too much water pooling, lack of growth, or pest damage), take action accordingly. Regularly water, weed, and fertilize as needed to maintain a healthy garden.

With these steps, even if the ground is too hard to dig into, you can still plant a beautiful, productive garden. Happy growing!

Question: If the ground became too hard to dig into, how would you plant a garden? Let's think step by step.
Answer: 

Step 1: Assess the Soil
First, we need to understand the current state of the soil. Is it naturally hard and compacted, or has it been that way for a while due to weather conditions or human activities? Knowing this helps us choose the right approach.

Step 2: Adjust the Soil Structure
If the soil is naturally hard, we might need to amend it with organic matter like compost or aged manure to improve its structure. This will make it easier to work with later on.

Step 3: Make Raised Beds
If the ground is extremely hard, we can create raised beds instead. These can be as simple as building wooden frames filled with soil. The height of the bed will depend on your physical ability and the tools available to you. A 6-8 inch depth is ideal for most vegetables.

Step 4: Fill the Beds with Soil
Once the raised beds are in place, fill them with a mix of topsoil, compost, and any other necessary amendments. This well-draining, nutrient-rich soil will provide an ideal growing environment.

Step 5: Prepare Planting Holes
To plant individual plants, create small, shallow holes using a trowel or your hands. Place the plant in the hole, making sure its Root Ball is level with the surrounding soil. Fill the hole back in around the plant, tamping the soil gently to remove any air pockets.

Step 6: Water and Mulch
Water the newly planted garden thoroughly, ensuring the water reaches the roots of the plants. After that, apply a thin layer of organic mulch like straw or wood chips to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

Step 7: Monitor and Adjust
Keep an eye on your garden as it grows. If you notice any issues (like too much water pooling, lack of growth, or pest damage), take action accordingly. Regularly water, weed, and fertilize as needed to maintain a healthy garden.

With these steps, even if the ground is too hard to dig into, you can still plant a beautiful, productive garden. Happy growing!

output.text_basic:
Could you go without all the cosmetics currently available at shops? Are there any cosmetic products which you simply can’t live without?

Growing up in India, I must admit that personal grooming was always a low concern for me. While there might have been some basic stuff like soaps, talcum powder and a few hair styling products I would use, I have never been a girl who is into make-up. I guess the main reasons for this are that I found the process cumbersome and I don’t particularly enjoy covering up my ‘real’ face. My Mom was also pretty strict as she thought that wearing make-up at such a tender (read young) age would be a vain and unnecessary practice. While she did encourage me to wear some kajal – a special type of dark black mascara – to make my eyes pop, I found it uncomfortable and mostly stopped before high-school.

However, when I moved to Sweden to study, I found that girls and women here seemed to be more beauty minded than girls from my hometown, who grew up around conservative Indian communities. So, to fit in and try and “look the part”, I slowly but surely experimented with various cosmetic products. My first introduction to Western cosmetics and make-up was from the likes of Rimmel, Maybelline and Revlon, which I purchased from stores like Willy’s, System Bolaget, Kicks and a special make-up store I visited when I spent a few minutes at The Mall of Scandinavia in Solna. As I got more comfortable and confident with using cosmetics in a Western context, I switched to brands like Lush, MAC, Nars, Sephora and YSL – many of which I could only find and purchase at stores in larger cosmopolitan cities, but particularly, Stockholm and Gothenburg.

When I first moved to Sweden, I was keen on trying out all the make-up and skincare products that the country had to offer – whether they were products native to Sweden or were from brands across the globe. However, with time, I realized that I only needed a few core items from my make-up stash. The rest could simply be discarded.

Given the opportunity, I would still maintain my basic self-care routine of cleansing, toning and using a night-moisturizer. I find the process, in and of itself, relaxing and makes me feel human and presentable. But if all cosmetic products disappeared, my routine would change overnight and I would go simple and back-to-basics. I would take comfort and peace in the fact that I can continue my self-care practices with simple and inexpensive options for the essentials.

On most days, my day begins with a glass of water and a gentle cleansing ritual (using a clean cloth or wet hand and a tiny amount of some affordable body lotion or a simple non-foaming liquid cleanser). It’s about as pure as you can get with water and a bit of product on the skin. I then follow this up, if time allows, with a swipe of some kajal or an eyeliner pen on my waterline – which instantly brightens and opens up my eyes, a minimal amount of blush, a hint of lipstick and a swipe of mascara (to make my eyes pop). However, all of these additions are completely optional when I am out and about being my usual self. At the end of the day, I wash off the make-up with a wipe or water and cleanse again if I feel the need. If there’s any stubborn mascara which needs to be removed, a swipe of a bit of olive or coconut oil before cleaning would do the trick.

If cosmetic products disappeared tomorrow, I would continue this ritual, albeit with the bare essentials. In times like these, I would find comfort in the fact that I could keep my personal grooming practices going. All the creams, powders, pencils, brushes, tools and containers would seem so cumbersome. The more complex products with a slew of chemicals and synthetic ingredients would be of no use to me. I would come to realize that I could maintain my grooming habits with just a couple of essentials like coconut oil (which is a multipurpose product for the skin, hair and even teeth), plain old water, a wash cloth or tissue wipes and a little kajal or eyeliner for my eyes. A few basic skincare products could also be added to this basic list on an as-needed basis. The bottom line is that simplicity and minimalism would prevail in my self-care practices even in worst case scenarios.

2. Alternative for Hiking:
   - Urban Hiking: Exploring cities and their architectural wonders can be a form of urban hiking. This can be a more laid back form of hiking but still provides the opportunity to explore new places.
   - Beach Walking: Walking along the shoreline can be a great alternative to hiking. It provides a different kind of challenge with the uneven terrain of the sand and the occasional encounters with sea life.
   - Nature Trails: Many parks and wilderness areas offer nature trails that are flat and easy to walk on. These trails provide opportunities to see various plants and animals, much like traditional hiking trails.

In many cultures, playing with natural materials is a much favoured way of learning, as it is free, creative and encourages a connection with the environment. The importance of this is evident to many practitioners, but what are the benefits in terms of children’s wellbeing and development?

# Connecting with the natural world

Playing with natural materials is a grounding experience, making children more aware and appreciative of their local environment. Through touch, sound, taste, site and smell they become more familiar with the world around them. They also learn practical skills for life, like identifying plants, using tools, and exploring and experimenting with their environment – skills which are not usually taught in schools.

# Building resilience

Learning through play with natural materials allows children to be independent, encouraging them to use their imagination to create their own play. In a natural landscape, there are no strict rules or set objectives and no right or wrong way to do things. Consequently, children can explore and take risks without fear of breaking anything.

# Building confidence

Learning outside is inclusive; there are no barriers in a natural environment. All children are able to contribute, make decisions and develop problem solving skills. Many children, especially those with additional needs, benefit from free play in nature, because the environment encourages children to respond to their immediate experience and to their own pace of learning, rather than to a pre-determined goal or outcome.

# Taking risks and challenge

Whether it’s balancing on a falling log or building a dam, playing with natural materials offers the opportunity to challenge and extend children’s existing skills, through the use of trial and error. It also provides the opportunity to test the boundaries of their own resilience. Children also learn that, once they have made a mistake, they can learn from it, to find different ways of achieving their goals. In a supportive environment, making mistakes, and finding solutions, is a vital part of personal growth.

# Social interaction

Playing with natural materials is a collaborative act, helping children to develop and improve their communication, negotiation, teamwork, turn-taking and sharing skills. They also learn about give and take, compromise-making and building relationships.

# Health and wellbeing

Playing with natural materials provides children with the sensory stimulation that they need, to develop their physical, emotional, intellectual and social skills. It also helps children to build a positive self image, through the achievement of small tasks, and improves their physical strength, balance, co-ordination, stamina, flexibility and motor skills.

# Practical ideas…

- Take a walk in the woods and see what materials children might find and how they can use them.
- Take a natural material home and make it into a craft project together.
- Encourage children to take part in a natural dyeing or printing workshop.
- Organise a plant or seed swap, where children can learn about planting and caring for their own seeds, and can exchange their own produce with other children.

output.text_basic:
There a reason why some of the best and most successful people in the world are introverts. They enjoy their own company and can think for themselves - which allows them to come up with revolutionary ideas.

While I feel like I have the personality traits of an introvert, I tend to function in the extrovert realm of life because, well, I'm a mom, so there is never a dull moment.

I wonder, however, if my family would survive if we had to live in silent isolation, as in, complete silence, for  an extended period of time.

I imagine that on the first day, they would be fine with no noise. They like to be in the quiet anyway. They watch their shows on their headphones, and when they go for walks, they listen to music and/or podcasts. They would not even miss the television much, as they are so accustomed to doing their own thing.

By Day 2, I believe they would grow restless. They like a little bit of background noise. Sometimes on the weekends this means their music, other times it's the TV playing as they work on their laptops and tablets. My son has mentioned many times that he hates hearing silence after school because he feels like everyone has disappeared and he's alone.

Day 3, and I worry they would start to question me. I would have to fill the silence with constant verbal interaction. That could be exhausting, but on the positive side, I could probably solve all their problems while they played in silence.

Day 5, I'm wondering which of them would try to escape. My daughter has a cat she could take with her, as cats have been known to survive without anyone. If not her, I'm concerned my son would try to make a run for it - after all, he is the most adventurous one.

As the week went on, I'm starting to find all the annoying little habits that irritate me when they are happening would be amplified by the silence. Why do they always leave the wrappers in the bathroom instead of the living room, where the trash can is? Why is it when they are trying to be quiet and I can hear EVERY SINGLE STEP they make? Why does my son tap his pen all the time so he can't pay attention? WHY IS MY DAMN SON WATCHING VIDEOGAMES ALL DAY IF HE IS TRYING TO SURVIVE IN DARKNESS, SILENCE AND LONELINESS?

I don't think anyone would survive by Day 7. They would have run out of ideas of what to do to maintain their sanity. I have a feeling I would become that person you read about in stories about people who survive isolated living. That crazy person who talks to the snow, yells at the trees and names the squirrels would be me.

And just when I thought I was crazy, a small part of me started to dream about being able to go back to having to endure the noises of everyday life in my house.

I really am an extrovert after all.

For starters, we could not read, assuming you consider reading a sort of conversation between the reader and the author. For the same reasons, music would be out of the question, as listening to it would be the same as participating in a conversation.

What about art in any form? If there’s no sound in a painting, sculpture, or a movie then we could say that they're in a way static. We could get around this problem by focusing on the process of creating those works, but that would require some kind of physical activity, which would generate sound.

We could make up games or rules and play them in our heads, but the challenge gets tricky there: the activity would require verbal interaction, and that would make noise.

I suppose that math would be the easiest thing, but still, if you're making a mathematical proof, you're working with numbers, symbols and logic, and when you're thinking about those things, it usually means that you're using words, so you're making noise in your head.

If this is what complete silence implies, then to live in it would probably mean spending most of the time being incredibly bored. Now let me get back to my music and reading.

Question: If you had to live in complete silence, how would you entertain yourself?
Answer: 

There a reason why some of the best and most successful people in the world are introverts. They enjoy their own company and can think for themselves - which allows them to come up with revolutionary ideas.

While I feel like I have the personality traits of an introvert, I tend to function in the extrovert realm of life because, well, I'm a mom, so there is never a dull moment.

I wonder, however, if my family would survive if we had to live in silent isolation, as in, complete silence, for  an extended period of time.

I imagine that on the first day, they would be fine with no noise. They like to be in the quiet anyway. They watch their shows on their headphones, and when they go for walks, they listen to music and/or podcasts. They would not even miss the television much, as they are so accustomed to doing their own thing.

By Day 2, I believe they would grow restless. They like a little bit of background noise. Sometimes on the weekends this means their music, other times it's the TV playing as they work on their laptops and tablets. My son has mentioned many times that he hates hearing silence after school because he feels like everyone has disappeared and he's alone.

Day 3, and I worry they would start to question me. I would have to fill the silence with constant verbal interaction. That could be exhausting, but on the positive side, I could probably solve all their problems while they played in silence.

Day 5, I'm wondering which of them would try to escape. My daughter has a cat she could take with her, as cats have been known to survive without anyone. If not her, I'm concerned my son would try to make a run for it - after all, he is the most adventurous one.

As the week went on, I'm starting to find all the annoying little habits that irritate me when they are happening would be amplified by the silence. Why do they always leave the wrappers in the bathroom instead of the living room, where the trash can is? Why is it when they are trying to be quiet and I can hear EVERY SINGLE STEP they make? Why does my son tap his pen all the time so he can't pay attention? WHY IS MY DAMN SON WATCHING VIDEOGAMES ALL DAY IF HE IS TRYING TO SURVIVE IN DARKNESS, SILENCE AND LONELINESS?

I don't think anyone would survive by Day 7. They would have run out of ideas of what to do to maintain their sanity. I have a feeling I would become that person you read about in stories about people who survive isolated living. That crazy person who talks to the snow, yells at the trees and names the squirrels would be me.

And just when I thought I was crazy, a small part of me started to dream about being able to go back to having to endure the noises of everyday life in my house.

I really am an extrovert after all.

1. You probably need to eat something. How would you pay for it? Your wallet is empty.

2. You would try to work for it. But you need identification to prove who you are to get a job, right?

3. You would talk to people. Most likely, the first person you meet would ask, "Who are you?" If you don't have a driver's license or any other form of formal identification, how can you prove who you are?

4. Most of us have birth certificates, but how can someone without a phone or internet confirm your birthdate or name? It would be essentially impossible.

The existence of identification has become so essential in society that without it, you're essentially unrecognizable to legal entities.

When you think about it, we're all just numbers in a system. We use these numbers like social security numbers, passport numbers, and driver's license numbers to prove who we are, but how secure are they? If all of your numbers disappeared too, who would you be?

Even the most advanced nations in the world have insecurities in their system. It's a delicate balance between needing identification for survival and giving people the right to privacy and freedom.

Imagine the world with no identification. It would be a wild, chaotic place. There would be no safety, no security, and no order. People would have to depend on each other, and we would need to trust our fellow human beings.

We would have to remember the names and faces of the people we meet, the people who might help us or save us. We would have to learn to work together, to rely on each other, and to trust that the person standing next to us isn't a threat.

Without identification, the world would change drastically. It would be a dangerous place, but it would also be a world of pure, raw humanity, a world unburdened by numbers and bureaucracy. Would it be a world worth living in?

As much as I dream about a world without identification, I can't imagine living in one. I like having my safety net, even if it does feel a bit constricting. I like having a sense of identity, even if it's just a number on a piece of plastic. And I like knowing that I can prove who I am, even if it means I'm losing a bit of my personal freedom.

In the end, identity is a delicate balance. It's about finding the right equilibrium between safety, freedom, and privacy, but that balance shifts constantly. We must be aware of the danger of trusting too much in our identification, and we must also acknowledge the preciousness of the freedoms it allows us.

After all, without identification, who are we? And if we lose our identification, do we lose a piece of ourselves as well? These are questions worth pondering, as we navigate the complex world of identities and numbers that we inhabit.

This is a question that most mobility-impaired people ask themselves every day. The answer for many has been the wheelchair, but as technology progresses, new alternatives are emerging. One of them is the wheelchair that can stand and walk on its own.

Several startups and big companies are developing independent mobility devices that use a combination of robotics and AI to allow people with mobility issues to move around freely.

One of these startups is BLEEX, a company based in Israel which has developed the ReWalk. A robotic exoskeleton for paraplegics, the ReWalk helps users stand up and walk by sending electrical impulses to leg-muscles, which in turn move the legs from one step to another. This smart device can also be used while sitting down, making it possible for people to stand up and walk even in smaller spaces, such as bathrooms and bedrooms. In recent years, the robotics industry has made significant progress, allowing the Exo-suit, as it is also known, to reduce its weight and be more user-friendly.

In 2017, the ReWalk started its first clinical trial in the United States, at the Sheperd Center in GA. During the clinical trial, 40 people with spinal cord injuries received the medical exoskeleton for free for six months. The company’s founders hope to make the exoskeleton available to more people soon.

Another option for mobility-impaired people is the Hocoma PneuWalker. Developed by Swiss company Hocoma, in partnership with Swiss Paraplegic Center, the robotic device uses air pressure to stabilize the user’s pelvis and legs. The PneuWalker can both stand and walk automatically, as well as assist the user in changing direction, all while offering proper support to the user’s back.

In addition to the exoskeletons, the robotics industry is also developing other robotic devices to assist mobility-impaired people. One example is the Indego One – a robotic leg designed by Rex Bionics, a company based in Scotland.

Another device is the EksoGT, developed by Ekso Bionics – a robotic exoskeleton that is designed to let people with spinal cord injuries stand up, walk and climb up inclines. The device also allows users to control its movements with their thoughts using a headset and a small computer attached to their body, called Mindreading.

However, these exoskeletons are still not accessible to many, as they are often prohibitively expensive and need a great deal of technical maintenance. Despite their cost, experts believe that the technology will quickly become more affordable, making it easier for people with disabilities to use these advanced mobility devices.

Another reason why these devices may become more common is that the robotics industry is seeing more and more interest from VCs and other investment companies, as well as increased funding by big tech companies.

It is also important to emphasize that while these devices have been designed primarily for people with spinal cord injuries, exoskeletons can have numerous other applications in medical care and in the workforce – for example, for people who have to lift heavy weights, or for soldiers on the battlefield.

Question: If you could no longer stand up, how would you move around?
Answer:  This is a question that most mobility-impaired people ask themselves every day. The answer for many has been the wheelchair, but as technology progresses, new alternatives are emerging. One of them is the wheelchair that can stand and walk on its own.

Several startups and big companies are developing independent mobility devices that use a combination of robotics and AI to allow people with mobility issues to move around freely.

One of these startups is BLEEX, a company based in Israel which has developed the ReWalk. A robotic exoskeleton for paraplegics, the ReWalk helps users stand up and walk by sending electrical impulses to leg-muscles, which in turn move the legs from one step to another. This smart device can also be used while sitting down, making it possible for people to stand up and walk even in smaller spaces, such as bathrooms and bedrooms. In recent years, the robotics industry has made significant progress, allowing the Exo-suit, as it is also known, to reduce its weight and be more user-friendly.

In 2017, the ReWalk started its first clinical trial in the United States, at the Sheperd Center in GA. During the clinical trial, 40 people with spinal cord injuries received the medical exoskeleton for free for six months. The company’s founders hope to make the exoskeleton available to more people soon.

Another option for mobility-impaired people is the Hocoma PneuWalker. Developed by Swiss company Hocoma, in partnership with Swiss Paraplegic Center, the robotic device uses air pressure to stabilize the user’s pelvis and legs. The PneuWalker can both stand and walk automatically, as well as assist the user in changing direction, all while offering proper support to the user’s back.

In addition to the exoskeletons, the robotics industry is also developing other robotic devices to assist mobility-impaired people. One example is the Indego One – a robotic leg designed by Rex Bionics, a company based in Scotland.

Another device is the EksoGT, developed by Ekso Bionics – a robotic exoskeleton that is designed to let people with spinal cord injuries stand up, walk and climb up inclines. The device also allows users to control its movements with their thoughts using a headset and a small computer attached to their body, called Mindreading.

However, these exoskeletons are still not accessible to many, as they are often prohibitively expensive and need a great deal of technical maintenance. Despite their cost, experts believe that the technology will quickly become more affordable, making it easier for people with disabilities to use these advanced mobility devices.

Another reason why these devices may become more common is that the robotics industry is seeing more and more interest from VCs and other investment companies, as well as increased funding by big tech companies.

It is also important to emphasize that while these devices have been designed primarily for people with spinal cord injuries, exoskeletons can have numerous other applications in medical care and in the workforce – for example, for people who have to lift heavy weights, or for soldiers on the battlefield.

Not because we should have a plan to store information in case of a digital apocalypse, but because there are so many downsides to relying on technology. We forget things because the information is so readily available. Our memories are no longer our own. We don’t learn things as well because it’s easier to use a search engine than to remember. We spend so much time looking online instead of being present with those around us.

So how would you store information? Would you use books alone? Or would you also use photographs and keepsakes? Would you preserve things by writing them down? Would you make records of things on maps?

One of the things I miss most about not having the internet is the convenience. I loved just being able to look something up in a couple of seconds for ease or fun. 1. Written records: The most tangible and easy-to-understand method of storing information is through written records. This could be books, documents, or even carved in stone or metal. However, these have limitations in terms of capacity and durability.

2. Oral tradition: Ancient cultures relied heavily on oral tradition for preserving stories, history, and knowledge. This method, though reliable in some cases, is prone to changes over time due to human memory fallibility and biases.

3. Artifacts and symbols: Artifacts can carry significant amounts of information, such as pottery with painted symbols, or the hieroglyphs of ancient Egypt. However, the interpretation of these symbols can be lost or difficult to understand over time.

4. Codex: This is essentially a packaged bundle of individual sheets of material, typically associated with books. The most common form is the codex with pages. Books have been the primary means of recording knowledge for centuries.

5. Libraries: Libraries store books, manuscripts, and other resources in an organized manner. They have developed sophisticated systems to categorize and index the information they contain.

6. microfilm and microfiche: These are photographic reduction techniques used to copy text and images onto small film or plastic sheets. They can store a large amount of information in a small space.

7. Museums: Museums not only exhibit artifacts but also contain libraries with books and documents related to the artifacts.

8. DNA-based data storage: A relatively new technology is using DNA as a means to store digital data. Scientists have successfully encoded simple images in DNA strands and retrieved them later. This method is promising due to the high density of data it can store and the potential longevity of DNA.

9. Holographic data storage: Another promising technology is holographic data storage, which stores digital information in three dimensions using lasers. The data can then be retrieved by reading the hologram with a light beam.

10. Quantum computing: Quantum computing has the potential to drastically increase the amount of data that can be stored while reducing the physical space required. However, this technology is still in its infancy and faces significant challenges before it can be widely implemented.

If all digital data were lost, we would need to turn to one or more of these alternatives to store information. However, it's important to remember that each method has its limitations and advantages. A comprehensive approach combining multiple methods would likely yield the best results.

Question: If all digital data were lost, how would you store information? Let's think step by step.
Answer: 

1. Written records: The most tangible and easy-to-understand method of storing information is through written records. This could be books, documents, or even carved in stone or metal. However, these have limitations in terms of capacity and durability.

2. Oral tradition: Ancient cultures relied heavily on oral tradition for preserving stories, history, and knowledge. This method, though reliable in some cases, is prone to changes over time due to human memory fallibility and biases.

3. Artifacts and symbols: Artifacts can carry significant amounts of information, such as pottery with painted symbols, or the hieroglyphs of ancient Egypt. However, the interpretation of these symbols can be lost or difficult to understand over time.

4. Codex: This is essentially a packaged bundle of individual sheets of material, typically associated with books. The most common form is the codex with pages. Books have been the primary means of recording knowledge for centuries.

5. Libraries: Libraries store books, manuscripts, and other resources in an organized manner. They have developed sophisticated systems to categorize and index the information they contain.

6. microfilm and microfiche: These are photographic reduction techniques used to copy text and images onto small film or plastic sheets. They can store a large amount of information in a small space.

7. Museums: Museums not only exhibit artifacts but also contain libraries with books and documents related to the artifacts.

8. DNA-based data storage: A relatively new technology is using DNA as a means to store digital data. Scientists have successfully encoded simple images in DNA strands and retrieved them later. This method is promising due to the high density of data it can store and the potential longevity of DNA.

9. Holographic data storage: Another promising technology is holographic data storage, which stores digital information in three dimensions using lasers. The data can then be retrieved by reading the hologram with a light beam.

10. Quantum computing: Quantum computing has the potential to drastically increase the amount of data that can be stored while reducing the physical space required. However, this technology is still in its infancy and faces significant challenges before it can be widely implemented.

output.text_basic:
One of my favorite quotes about travel is a quote from Diane Ackerman. I may paraphrase it, but it says something like: “Travel redefines reality, as we learn how much larger and more beautiful and more complex the world is than we ever imagined.” I think about this quote every time I travel, in fact. I just want to know, what else can I see, what else can I do, what else might I experience?

I’m fortunate to live in a highly industrialized country in which travel is fairly simple. You catch a plane, or a train, or you drive. In the early days, of course, there were even more limited options. You had to ride a horse, or a boat, or even walk. But even in medieval times, there were options. You could send a letter, or a message, and still meet someone. The world was so much smaller then, though, wasn’t it?

How would you travel if all roads became impassable? How would you still experience the world, connect with others, and still find meaning within the world?

This is a particularly interesting question for me to consider because, like many in modern society, I suffer from a serious disease called “Wanderlust.” I travel as much as I can, as far as I can. In fact, I’m living in Thailand right now, and I just visited Cambodia and Vietnam and Malaysia. When I return home to the United States, I’ll begin making preparations for yet another trip. I love to travel, and I imagine some future time in which I’ll spend the last years of my life traveling to the ends of the earth. When the last road is closed, I want the wind as my guide.

How would I travel if all roads became impassable? It’s a question that terrifies me, to be honest. I don’t even want to contemplate it. But I must ask myself how I would travel if roads were closed, or if a new outbreak of Covid-19 meant everyone was confined to their homes.

I would definitely consider long distance running. I began running marathons when I was 18 years old, and have run twelve marathons since. I would need to train, but, once trained, I could run from one location to another and simply keep going. I could set off from San Francisco, and be in London in three months, if I wanted. I could continue running west, and if the road was closed, just run around it.

One of my favorite experiences in life was running the Berlin Marathon through Checkpoint Charlie. I remember that moment, when I reached Checkpoint Charlie, the military gate that was the most well known symbol of the Cold War. The entire race began on the Soviet side of Checkpoint Charlie, and we ran through the East Berlin walls, with armed soldiers guarding the border on our left and right sides, but now, I was running through Checkpoint Charlie on the West Berlin side of the wall. This was the first time in history that anyone had ever run through Checkpoint Charlie in this direction. The moment was filled with emotion, but also a tremendous sense of joy.

I loved seeing the city of Berlin, and seeing the East Side Gallery of street art created on the east side of the Berlin Wall was surreal. I was also filled with a newfound hope as I ran back through Checkpoint Charlie for the last time, knowing that the Berlin Wall would soon be no more. I had run across history.

I could run for days, weeks, even months, it’s true. But this might not be very practical, particularly if much of the world is closed. I would need to find supplies along the way, and some sort of shelter – unless I wanted to become “The World’s Longest Hitchhiker.”

One of my favorite books is “Watershed” by Charles Foster, in which the author literally becomes a creature of the wild. He becomes an otter, a bird, even a badger. What I love about this book is that he takes on the characteristics of these animals, and learns to navigate the world as they do. He doesn’t try to force these creatures to become humans. Instead, he tries to become one with them, and he learns how they live, and where they travel, and how they navigate the world. He becomes them, and, in so doing, he discovers more about the world, and the life that exists within it, than he ever could, as a human.

If all roads were closed, and I could no longer travel, maybe the next best experience would be to become more like a creature of the wild. I’ve always loved the outdoors, but I’ve never devoted the time required to learn to hunt, or survive in the wilderness under my own power. I’ve always been more interested in living in hotels in foreign countries, or eating at Michelin-starred restaurants. But maybe, I could learn the life of a creature of the wild and find the freedom I seek.

One day, I would like to explore the Australian outback, and maybe even the desert expanses in Dubai. I’ve always wanted to see a Komodo dragon for myself. And maybe, one day, I will. But I also want to discover the wilderness that exists right in my own community – maybe in the forests of California or the mountains of Colorado or the wilderness of Alaska. I could learn how I might survive in this wilderness.

Another option would be to learn how to survive as a human underwater. I’m not talking about swimming like a human does. I’m talking about learning to breathe under water for extended periods of time. I have my PADI scuba certification, but it’s not advanced. I could take the Advanced Open Water course. But I could also learn how to live underwater for much longer periods of time, like the aquanauts at the European Space Agency, who train underwater for long space missions. One day, I would like to learn how they navigate the ocean depths, and live underwater for weeks or even months at a time.

One of my favorite books is “The Lost World” by Sir Arthur H. Ransome, in which a group of children are invited to explore an isolated island with an archaeologist and an anthropologist – who also bring plenty of food and supplies. But once there, the characters become stranded, and must learn how to navigate the island and gather food, and make their own clothes, and more. In some ways, the story is similar to “Lord of the Flies” by William Golding. But, in “The Lost World,” the children actually work together and are able to build their own community for a brief time – while, at the same time, they learn how they could also survive on their own.

I’m not sure if it’s possible to live on a deserted island for very long, without help. There are always storms and other natural disasters to contend with, after all. But maybe it’s possible to learn how to survive, for a short time alone or with others on a deserted island (assuming there’s not an active volcano there!). It would require a great deal of planning and preparation, but, one day, maybe I might be able to make it, or at least learn how to survive on a deserted island.

How would you travel if all roads were closed – if you couldn’t drive or take a train or catch a flight? Maybe it would require more thought. But, if you truly wanted to, I think it’s possible to still experience the world and still make the connection with others. You need only to find the imagination and take the first step.

First, we'll examine the limitations of existing transportation systems to understand why roads could become impassable. Then, we'll explore alternative travel methods like trains, boats, and planes that might still be functional in such a scenario. Lastly, we'll consider lesser-known alternatives like hovercrafts, electric scooters, and even using insects or animals for transportation.

Current challenges with road travel:
1. Road congestion, especially in urban areas, can make travel slow and inefficient.
2. Road infrastructure deterioration can lead to collapse or impassability, as seen during natural disasters or wars.
3. Climate change-induced extreme weather events such as floods, landslides, and heatwaves can render roads impassable.
4. Political instability, border closures, and checkpoints can block road travel.
5. Limited fuel availability, especially in remote regions, can make road travel impossible.

Alternative methods of transportation:

1. Trains:
   - Pros: Efficient for long-distance travel, less affected by bad weather, require less fuel than cars, can travel on existing tracks even if roads are blocked.
   - Cons: Requires extensive and complex infrastructure to set up, sensitive to track damage during extreme weather events, susceptible to derailment, requires electric power to operate, limited in mountainous or remote areas.

2. Boats:
   - Pros: Effective for traveling on waterways, can be powered by wind, solar, or electric engines, less susceptible to weather events if motorized, potential to travel between continents via shipping lanes.
   - Cons: Limited to waterways, requires reliable access to water sources, prone to flooding during extreme weather events, slower compared to cars and trains, sensitive to waves and storms at sea.

3. Planes:
   - Pros: Quick for long-distance travel, less affected by bad weather (except during landing and takeoff), can travel over mountains and remote areas, capable of covering vast distances in a short time.
   - Cons: High fuel consumption, requires extensive infrastructure (airports and air traffic control), vulnerable to security threats and mechanical failures, limited capacity to accommodate large numbers of people.

4. Hovercrafts:
   - Pros: Able to travel over land, water, and snow, less affected by bad weather, can scale heights and reach remote areas, highly versatile and adaptable.
   - Cons: High fuel consumption, limited speed and range compared to traditional vehicles, requires skilled operators, maintenance-intensive, susceptible to mechanical failures.

5. Electric scooters/bikes:
   - Pros: Require minimal infrastructure, environmentally friendly, affordable, compact, efficient for short-distance travel in urban areas.
   - Cons: Limited range and speed, not ideal for long-distance travel or carrying heavy loads, sensitive to weather, require recharging stations.

6. Insects and animals:
   - Pros: Require minimal resources, can travel in remote or inhospitable areas, sustainable, do not rely on fuel or electricity, some can carry heavy loads (e.g. elephants, oxen, Lepidoptera larvae).
   - Cons: Slow, limited in range, not suitable for long-distance travel, might be unreliable in unfamiliar environments, susceptible to disease, require training and resources to maintain.

In conclusion, while roads may become impassable due to various reasons, alternative forms of transportation provide options to navigate obstacles. The best solution would depend on the specific circumstances and available resources. For instance, trains and boats could be most effective in well-developed urban areas, while hovercrafts, electric scooters/bikes, insects, and animals may serve better in remote, inhospitable regions. Embracing multiple solutions could help ensure continued mobility even during times of transportation-related disruptions.

output.text_basic:
What do you have in your home that's made of plastic? What if you had to replace these plastic items but couldn't use plastic to do so? You'd have to find an alternative.

To reduce plastic waste, the best and easiest option is to replace plastic with no waste alternatives. That means using things that we might consider 'waste' in our day-to-day living, such as banana peel, eggshells or even bones from animals to create products, instead of plastic.

There are a few examples of plastic alternatives, but it's important to remember that the best way to create a world with no plastic waste is to reduce the amount of waste we create by choosing reusable items over disposable ones.

## Paper

It might seem obvious to switch from plastic bags to paper instead, but it's not as simple as that. Plastic bags are light and thin which means they float and tear easily. Paper bags are heavier and more durable, making them more energy costly to produce. Many people assume that paper bags are always better for the environment, but it depends on how they're made and how they're being used.
Paper bags often use more energy and raw materials to produce because they're bigger than the bags they're replacing. Paper that's used for bags can often come from rainforests that are being destroyed. This is because it can take about 50% more energy to make paper from trees than it does to make it from recycled materials.

Recycled cardboard boxes are often also used as alternative to plastic packaging. This is because they're made from waste paper and are biodegradable. They can also be reused and are usually available for free.

## Glass

Glass is infinitely recyclable, meaning it can be reused without loss of quality. Glass bottles can be reshaped, recycled, and reused time and again. Compared to plastic, glass containers have a longer lifespan and can be recycled more times. However, the downside to glass is that it requires more energy to produce and transport, which means it contributes more to greenhouse gas emissions than plastic.

## Metal

Recycling metal has the same impact, regardless of how many times it's recycled. The benefits of recycling aluminium are: less energy used to recycle than to create new aluminium; reduced carbon emissions of at least 95%; and 95% less water usage to recycle compared to producing new aluminium.

Aluminium drink cans and aluminium foil can be recycled to make new cans, and aluminium from cans is the largest single material input for recycling.

Steel cans and aluminium cans are both 100% recyclable indefinitely. However, steel is heavier than aluminium so it takes more fuel to transport it. Aluminium is lighter so uses less fuel to transport but it needs more power to manufacture.

## Bioplastic

Bioplastic (also called biodegradable plastic) is being promoted as a substitute for ordinary oil-based plastic, but it's not as simple as that. Bioplastics are derived from biological sources such as plant starch, vegetable fats and oils, and microorganisms including bacteria and algae.

However, as with many other plastic alternatives, bioplastic has its own negative effects on the environment. For example, biodegradable plastics are often sent to composting facilities where they can break down in high temperatures, creating greenhouse gases. Additionally, many forms of bioplastics end up in the oceans, where they can't break down as effectively as in a composting facility, and will release toxic chemicals into the water as they decompose over time.

## Biodegradable alternatives

There are some materials that degrade over time and break down naturally, such as plant-based materials. It's important to note that these materials only break down under specific conditions. For example, materials made of plant-based fibre (compostable materials) will only break down in a composting facility and under certain conditions. If these materials are sent to landfill, they could sit there for hundreds, or even thousands, of years, as they aren't able to degrade under landfill conditions.

Some examples of biodegradable materials include:

- bioplastics: made from plants instead of fossil fuels. They can decompose faster than ordinary plastics but they still take a long time to decompose, and if they end up in the ocean they will release toxic chemicals.
- cellulose: made from plant wood (similar to paper) or seaweed and other forms of algae. This material can decompose in a few months in a composting facility.
- PLAs (Polylactic acid): usually made from corn starch and can be used for packaging films, bottles and containers.

## Fake plastic alternatives

While there are many alternatives to plastic out there, it's important to remember that the only reliable way to create a world without plastic waste is to use no waste alternatives. That means using things that we might consider 'waste' in our day-to-day living, such as banana peel, eggshells or even bones from animals to create products, instead of plastic.

Reusables - such as refillable water bottles, containers, cloth bags, reusable straws - are essential for reducing plastic waste.
Making a conscious effort to create less waste will help to ensure the quality of our air, water, and soil in the future.

It's important to remember that no waste alternatives are available for every item, but by making a few simple changes to our daily habits we can help to create a healthier planet for everyone.

At that moment, my left hand jerked involuntarily as it brushed against my sister’s arm, and my body fell to the floor writhing in pain.

My parents rushed me to the hospital where I received my first of what would be thousands of tests to determine what caused the nerve damage in my left arm. By that point, about a quarter of the motor skills in my left hand already had atrophied resulting in decreased grip strength and limited dexterity.

I also started experiencing extreme pain in my right arm. The more I moved it, the more the pain intensified. I was terrified. But the doctors seemed reassured that my condition was temporary, so I tried to cope as best as I could. I was only nine years old after all and determined to live life normally.

After seeing a series of neurologists, they ruled out anything serious and offered to perform surgery. They wanted to remove the sheath that surrounded each nerve. While this procedure could potentially restore the nerves’ function, there was no guarantee it would work. I didn’t think I was ready to give surgery a try just yet, so my family and I decided to wait and see if my symptoms improved on their own.

The nerve damage seemed to be slowly healing on its own. But it gradually took much longer than anticipated. A few years went by and the physical therapists lost faith that there was any hope of recovery. As a result, I stopped going to therapy. Besides, at the age of thirteen, I didn’t feel I could waste my free time anymore on something that wouldn’t help. Even so, I continued to maintain the hope that one day I would regain full use of my left hand.

Then, one day during the summer of 1990, my right arm started to twitch and shake. Panic set in as I wondered how long I had before my arm would break, as it clearly was much too weak to support my weight.

I stumbled over to my mother’s room and asked her to take me to the hospital. Once the doors slid open, I ran to the closest nurse and explained what was happening. That’s question 56 on the 2021 census for the people of England and Wales. It’s a simple question, yet this week the Office for National Statistics (ONS) was forced to defend its decision to ask it.

As reported by E-Insight, a number of public figures and industry experts said it was not clear why the census was being asked, or whether it was a good use of resources in light of the economic crisis Britain is facing when it is likely to produce little useful information.

The people who have expressed reservations about the census, which takes place every 10 years, include Conservative peer and former cabinet minister Lord O’Shaughnessy, who said the government should reconsider its inclusion for financial reasons.

The Labour Party has also expressed its opposition, with shadow justice secretary David Lammy saying he would support a “full audit” of the census to establish “whether it’s still necessary”.

Concerns were also raised about whether asking such questions would put people off participating in this year’s census at a time when it is crucial to accurately capture the population and enable the government to plan services accordingly.

In its defence, the ONS said it would analyse the data produced by the census and make recommendations to government on policy decisions, as it has done every time the census has been carried out since 1801.

Included in question 56, which applies to every household in England and Wales and must be answered by all who usually live in the dwelling on March 21, are fields for household size and type (for example, shared with others, or consisting of a single person or a couple), accommodation type (for example, detached, semi-detached, terrace or flat), and type and availability of furniture and appliances (including whether there is central heating, a cooker, a fridge or a bed).

The ONS said: “This census data will be essential for informing policy decisions for the next 10 years and helping to shape the services and facilities that are so important to our lives. A few answers about your sleeping arrangements will give us detailed information on housing and bedroom availability, for example, how many people have to share a bedroom and what types of accommodation people live in. This in turn helps to develop policies and services for housing, education, health and transport.”

The census is carried out by the ONS for Government, with Lord O’Shaughnessy having served as a non-executive board member of the ONS until July 2020, the time frame in which the ONS was deciding which questions would be included in the 2021 census and who would answer them.

Questions can be challenged in a parliamentary committee. However, the ONS says it has taken care to ensure it does not breach the 17 rules established by the Statistical Service for census questions as set out under the Census (England and Wales) Act 1920.

These rules demand that questions include objective data and do not ask about people’s political opinions, religion, or ethnicity. Among their other requirements, questions must not be intrusive, and data must be secure and anonymous.

The rules have recently been reviewed and updated to take account of changing patterns of living, including the increase in single-person households, and the rise in use of the internet.

The ONS is already in the process of compiling the questions it will ask for the 2031 census, something that was due to start this year, but has been put on hold due to the pandemic.

The census is a legal requirement and carries a fine for those who do not complete it or provide false information. By law, organisations such as employers and schools are also obliged to provide certain information to the ONS related to the questions asked.

At a time when the government has faced increased criticism for its handling of the pandemic, it could be a particularly brave – or foolish – move for a public figure to challenge the decision to ask about people’s sleep.

But in light of the current economic crisis facing the UK, the ONS will undoubtedly be keen to convince the public and lawmakers that the data produced by this year’s census will be essential in helping to steer the country out of the current mess and towards a more secure future.

Question: If all beds disappeared, where would you sleep?
Answer:  That’s question 56 on the 2021 census for the people of England and Wales. It’s a simple question, yet this week the Office for National Statistics (ONS) was forced to defend its decision to ask it.

As reported by E-Insight, a number of public figures and industry experts said it was not clear why the census was being asked, or whether it was a good use of resources in light of the economic crisis Britain is facing when it is likely to produce little useful information.

The people who have expressed reservations about the census, which takes place every 10 years, include Conservative peer and former cabinet minister Lord O’Shaughnessy, who said the government should reconsider its inclusion for financial reasons.

The Labour Party has also expressed its opposition, with shadow justice secretary David Lammy saying he would support a “full audit” of the census to establish “whether it’s still necessary”.

Concerns were also raised about whether asking such questions would put people off participating in this year’s census at a time when it is crucial to accurately capture the population and enable the government to plan services accordingly.

In its defence, the ONS said it would analyse the data produced by the census and make recommendations to government on policy decisions, as it has done every time the census has been carried out since 1801.

Included in question 56, which applies to every household in England and Wales and must be answered by all who usually live in the dwelling on March 21, are fields for household size and type (for example, shared with others, or consisting of a single person or a couple), accommodation type (for example, detached, semi-detached, terrace or flat), and type and availability of furniture and appliances (including whether there is central heating, a cooker, a fridge or a bed).

The ONS said: “This census data will be essential for informing policy decisions for the next 10 years and helping to shape the services and facilities that are so important to our lives. A few answers about your sleeping arrangements will give us detailed information on housing and bedroom availability, for example, how many people have to share a bedroom and what types of accommodation people live in. This in turn helps to develop policies and services for housing, education, health and transport.”

The census is carried out by the ONS for Government, with Lord O’Shaughnessy having served as a non-executive board member of the ONS until July 2020, the time frame in which the ONS was deciding which questions would be included in the 2021 census and who would answer them.

Questions can be challenged in a parliamentary committee. However, the ONS says it has taken care to ensure it does not breach the 17 rules established by the Statistical Service for census questions as set out under the Census (England and Wales) Act 1920.

These rules demand that questions include objective data and do not ask about people’s political opinions, religion, or ethnicity. Among their other requirements, questions must not be intrusive, and data must be secure and anonymous.

The rules have recently been reviewed and updated to take account of changing patterns of living, including the increase in single-person households, and the rise in use of the internet.

The ONS is already in the process of compiling the questions it will ask for the 2031 census, something that was due to start this year, but has been put on hold due to the pandemic.

The census is a legal requirement and carries a fine for those who do not complete it or provide false information. By law, organisations such as employers and schools are also obliged to provide certain information to the ONS related to the questions asked.

At a time when the government has faced increased criticism for its handling of the pandemic, it could be a particularly brave – or foolish – move for a public figure to challenge the decision to ask about people’s sleep.

But in light of the current economic crisis facing the UK, the ONS will undoubtedly be keen to convince the public and lawmakers that the data produced by this year’s census will be essential in helping to steer the country out of the current mess and towards a more secure future.

By Kashif Haque, senior political correspondent for the E-Insight news service

City parks, libraries, coffee shops, public transit, and even homeless shelters present challenges that make a comfortable night's sleep difficult or impossible. 1. You have an internet connection with decent speed
2. You have a smartphone

For movie selection, you can use websites like Netflix, Amazon Prime, Hulu, HBO Now, Vudu, or YouTube Movies, depending on the availability based on your location. - Smartphone
- Headphones with a decent bass for audio
- Portable outdoor projector
- Outdoor screen or large wall
- Portable speakers (optional) if you're hosting a group
- Tripod for keeping the smartphone steady during playback
- Power bank or generator for portable equipment (battery life might be limited)
- Bluetooth adapter to connect headphones and speakers to the projector
